Pakistan's leadership stresses need for unity, reforms as nation celebrates Independence Day. Pakistan’s civilian and military leadership has stressed the need for unity and reforms as the nation celebrates 79 years of independence today. According to state-run Radio Pakistan , the day dawned with a 31-gun salute in Islamabad and a 21-gun salute at the provincial headquarters. A change of guards ceremony was also held at the mausoleum of Quaid-i-Azam Mohammad Ali Jinnah in Karachi. Flag hoisting ceremonies were also held at the Supreme Court and the Federal Constitutional Court in Islamabad. ‘Pakistan’s security linked to peace in our neighbourhood’ In his message, President Asif Ali Zardari paid tribute to Quaid-i-Azam, those behind the Pakistan Movement and those who sacrificed their homes, security and livelihoods in the struggle for a homeland. “But independence is not only a historic achievement. It is also a responsibility that each generation must carry forward. The Pakistan that was created through the democratic will of its people must continue to grow stronger, more secure and more prosperous. Our task is not only to remember what earlier generations achieved, but to add to it through our own work,” he said. The president said that the past year had reminded citizens of the strength of the Pakistani nation. Recalling last year’s brief military conflict with India, he said, “The events surrounding Marka-i-Haq demonstrated that Pakistan seeks peace, but also possesses the resolve and capacity to defend its sovereignty and national interests. The lesson of strength is ultimately a lesson of responsibility. A country that can defend itself must also use its strength to prevent conflict, protect peace and serve the interests of its people.” He said that the security and stability enjoyed today had come at a great cost, paying tribute to the martyrs of the armed forces, law enforcement agencies and police. “Their courage and commitment have helped safeguard our nation against external aggression and the threat of terrorism. The people of Pakistan remain deeply grateful for their service,” he said. He also highlighted Pakistan’s efforts to facilitate dialogue in the region. “Pakistan has effectively used its channels of communication, its geographical location and diplomatic capital to encourage dialogue and de-escalation at a time when wider conflict could have serious consequences for the region and the world,” he said. He reiterated that all disputes must be ultimately addressed through dialogue and diplomacy. “Our security is linked to the peace and stability of our neighbourhood and the world at large. Pakistan will continue to support efforts that reduce tensions, protect regional stability and create conditions for cooperation,” he said. The president also went on to say that the country must focus on the work that will determine Pakistan’s future. “We must strengthen our economy, create greater opportunities for our young people, improve education and skills, strengthen institutions through a series of governance, economic and social reforms to ensure that the benefits of development and democracy reach every part and community of the country,” he said. “Pakistan’s greatest strength is its young people. Across the country and around the world, they are demonstrating their talent in science, technology, business, education and the creative industries. Our responsibility is to give them the education, skills and opportunities they need to realise their potential. By investing in our youth today, we are investing in Pakistan’s future,” he added. “For ordinary Pakistanis, national progress is measured in practical terms. It means a young person finding the skills and opportunity to build a career. It means a family being able to access quality education and healthcare. It means farmers, workers, traders and businesses being able to plan for the future with greater confidence. The strength of Pakistan will ultimately be judged by whether our national progress improves the lives of its people,” President Zardari said. He also voiced Pakistan’s support for the people of occupied Kashmir, saying Pakistan will continue to support a peaceful resolution of the dispute in accordance with the aspirations of its people and the relevant United Nations resolutions. On Afghanistan, the president said that Pakistan had always respected and supported the national sovereignty of our neighbour Afghanistan and expected the same reciprocity. “It is sad that the current interim regime of Afghanistan is allowing and supporting a cocktail of terror groups to use their soil for launching attacks against neighbouring countries including Pakistan. It is sad the Taliban regime of Afghanistan is collaborating with India in launching terror attacks against Pakistani civilians and security personnel. They are doing this to distract us from the peace building efforts of Pakistan, recognised by the entire world,” he said. “I warn them to stop these evil actions against the people of Pakistan and assure all and sundry that the armed forces of Pakistan are capable of defeating these evil designs,” he said. He ended his message by calling on the nation to contribute to the country’s progress in whatever field they serve. ‘Pakistan committed to defending its national interests’ Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also began his message by paying tribute to the founding leaders of Pakistan, saying the nation owed the fulfilment of its dream of an independent homeland to their vision, statesmanship and sacrifices. Highlighting the government’s economic achievements over the past two-and-a-half years, PM Shehbaz said the country had successfully navigated challenging circumstances to achieve economic stability and was now moving towards becoming a developed economy. He noted that remittances from overseas Pakistanis had increased by $11.3 billion over the past two years, which he termed a reflection of their confidence in government policies. The prime minister said harnessing modern information technology, promoting innovation-driven industrial and agricultural development, creating employment opportunities and establishing a world-class education and skills system remained among the government’s top priorities. Paying tribute to the armed forces, the prime minister said the military, under the leadership of Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, had demonstrated exemplary unity and courage during Marka-i-Haq, adding another chapter to the country’s history of defence. He said Pakistan remained committed to defending its national interests, including its right to water resources, and reiterated that the country would continue to play its role as a responsible nation and a stabilising force for regional and global peace. He cited the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye as testimony to the country’s growing strategic role in the region. The prime minister also expressed solidarity with the people of occupied Kashmir and the Palestinian people. He said lasting peace in South Asia was contingent upon a diplomatic resolution of the Kashmir dispute in line with United Nations resolutions, international law and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people. The prime minister also paid tribute to the martyrs of the armed forces and law enforcement agencies who sacrificed their lives for the country, and called upon all segments of society, particularly political parties, to work together for national unity, integrity and the advancement of national interests. He concluded his message by praying for Pakistan’s continued progress and dignity in the comity of nations. ‘Pakistan’s strength lies in the unity of its people’ CDF Munir, Chief of Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf and Chief of Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Baber Sidhu also issued a message to mark Independence Day. According to Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the armed forces paid tribute to the Quaid and those whose sacrifices resulted in a sovereign Pakistan. “Their vision, courage and resolve remain a guiding force for the nation and continue to inspire us to uphold the principles and ideals of Pakistan,” the statement said. “The armed forces of Pakistan respectfully acknowledge the supreme sacrifices of our martyrs, the services of our veterans, the dedication of law enforcement personnel and the contributions of every Pakistani who has served the nation. Their courage and selfless service have bolstered Pakistan’s resilience and safeguarded its independence, security and national interests,” it added. “As guardians of Pakistan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, the armed forces reaffirm their unwavering resolve to defend the motherland against all threats, uphold the Constitution and discharge the sacred trust reposed in them by the people of Pakistan. United with the nation, the armed forces will remain steadfast in preserving peace and stability while creating an environment conducive to national progress and prosperity,” the statement said. “Pakistan’s strength lies in the unity and collective resolve of its people. On this Independence Day, let us renew our commitment to the enduring principles of faith, unity and discipline, strengthen national cohesion, promote tolerance and work together towards a secure, stable and prosperous Pakistan,” it concluded. Dar reaffirms determination to safeguard country’s sovereignty In his message on the occasion, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar recalled Marka-i-Haq and reaffirmed Pakistan’s determination to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity. “We commemorated the first anniversary of Marka-i-Haq, recalling Pakistan’s resolute and successful response to Indian aggression in 2025,” he said in a televised address to the nation. “The occasion reaffirmed our determination to safeguard Pakistan’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity while remaining firmly committed to international law, responsible state craft and the pursuit of regional peace.” At the outset of his address, the deputy PM extended greetings to Pakistanis and expatriates on the Independence Day, saying we commemorate the day “to pay tribute to Quaid-i-Azam whose visionary leadership, unwavering resolve and steadfast commitment transformed the aspirations for a separate homeland into reality”. He also paid honour to the leaders and workers of the Pakistan movement whose “courage, dedication and countless sacrifices laid the foundations of our independent state”. Dar said that since independence, the country had made “remarkable strides across diverse fields guided by the enduring principles of unity, faith and discipline”. “Today we are a resilient nation of more than 250 million people bound together by our shared history, collective heritage and common aspirations,” he added. He also noted that the country’s achievements in education, science and technology, economic development, sports, culture and other fields “reflect the talent, determination and immense potential of our people”. The deputy PM also mentioned Pakistan’s “strengthened” position on the international stage over the past eight decades. “Our expanding diplomatic engagement, growing economic connectivity and partnerships, and deepening defence and security cooperation reflect Pakistan’s confidence and its commitment to contributing to a peaceful, stable and prosperous region and world.” He also mentioned the defence accord signed by Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia last week, saying the “historic agreement reflects our shared resolve to deepen strategic cooperation, strengthen collective security and address evolving regional and international peace and security challenges”. He also paid special tribute to armed forces, police and paramilitary forces of the country, saying their “courage, professionalism and unwavering commitment remain a bulwark of our national security”. Dar noted the country always “stood for peace, dialogue, cooperation and mutual respect among nations”. He referred to last year’s conflict with India and said the events “underscored the urgent need of peaceful resolution of longstanding disputes, particularly the Jammu and Kashmir dispute which remains a source of instability in our region”. “Pakistan will continue to extend its principles, moral, political and diplomatic support to the Kashmiri people in their just struggle for the realisation of their right to self-determination in accordance with the relevant UNSC resolutions,” he added. On the occasion, he urged people to “draw renewed inspirations from the ideals and vision that led to the creation of Pakistan”. “Let us reaffirm our collective resolve to strengthen our institutions, uphold our national unity, harness the potential of our people and build a stronger more prosperous and peaceful Pakistan for generations to come,” he concluded. Kashmir stands ‘shoulder to shoulder’ with Pakistan: AJK president Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) President Chaudhry Latif Akbar, addressing a flag-hoisting ceremony in Muzafarabad, expressed gratitude to Pakistan for standing by the Kashmiri people and advocating their cause at international forums, as well as repeatedly calling for implementation of the relevant United Nations resolutions. He highlighted the “centuries-old” bonds between Kashmir and Pakistan, saying the relationship was rooted in shared history, culture, religion, traditions and aspirations and had found political expression in the Kashmiri leadership’s July 19, 1947, resolution seeking accession of the princely state to Pakistan. “Pakistan has also stood with the people of Kashmir through difficult periods and fought wars in defence of its position on the Kashmir dispute,” he said, adding that Kashmiris would never forget Pakistan’s steadfast support. Akbar reiterated that the people of AJK stood “shoulder to shoulder” with the people of Pakistan and said their destinies were intertwined. Additional input from Tariq Naqash

Footprints: SPEAKING URDU IN XINJIANG. Sunny (Rahiman Ma) in the front joins in a Mongolian folk dance during a visit to the Xianghe community in Urumqi. —Photo by the writer “ASSALAM-o-Alaikum Wa Rahmatullah-i-Wa Barakatuh.” This is how our tour guide greets us soon after landing at Urumqi Airport. She introduces herself as ‘Sunny’, and then tells us that her given name is Rahiman Ma. “You are Muslim?” I ask. “Alhamdolillah yes,” she smiles and nods. Urumqi, the capital and largest city in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region in Northwestern China, has an estimated population of 4.4 million people including a robust Muslim population of Uyghur, Hui, Mongols, Kazakh and Kyrgyz Muslims, that amounts to around 12 per cent of the city’s total number of people. Over the course of the next three days, I encounter many more Muslims in the city, as well as several others with Muslim-sounding names who said that they don’t follow any religion. I also notice some Arabic writing along with the Chinese Hanzi script on banners and boards, only to be informed that it is the Uyghur script that I’m seeing. I meet Dilnar and Yasmin Jahan, who say they are Uyghur but not Muslim. Dilnar has visited Islamabad and developed a liking for Pakistani food. Although Yasmin has not been to Pakistan, but she speaks excellent Urdu. She happily drops her real name, Lily, to proudly carry the name given to her by her Urdu teacher in Beijing. Women in this region usually retire at 55, while the men work for another five years Sunny, Dilnar and Yasmin accompany us to the Wu Yi Tongxiangdong Mosque in the 12th Division of the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps. It is a rural area surrounded by orchards and farms. Unlike everywhere else in China, there is no big electronic screen to introduce you to the place with a short documentary, nor is there a rotating Lazy Susan on the dining table. It is Friday afternoon. Chen Yun, the Imam of the mosque, offers you the bounties of nature and savoury items prepared by the mosque volunteers. “They were so looking forward to meeting you all that they delayed going home after Friday prayers to prepare this humble spread for you,” the Imam tells our delegation of journalists from Pakistan. Meanwhile, Sunny leans forward to ask me if women in Pakistan pray in mosques. I explained to her that we can be in some of our mosques, but not together. Just then, the Imam tells us that his mosque is also for men only. He also says that there are around 25,000 mosques in Xinjiang, but when I ask about the number of Imam Bargahs, he says: “None. The Muslims here are all Sunni”. On the urban side, the strikingly majestic Erdaoqiao Mosque is surrounded by the bustling Grand Bazaar, beckoning all, especially tourists. Noticing me peering into his shop of beaded jewellery more than once, the shopkeeper gestures for me to come inside, calling out: “Andar ajao Behen [Come in Sister]!” Not sure I heard him right, I ask if he just spoke in Urdu? “Haan haan [Yes yes],” he says. His name is Aziz and he picked up Urdu in Islamabad where he ran a shop around 15 years ago. “But that was a long time ago,” he says, adding that he is now permanently stationed in Urumqi. “I’m very happy with my life in China,” he tells me. That evening on our bus ride back to our hotel, Sunny sings to us. “It means: I love Xinjiang and Xinjiang loves me,” she translates. Does she really? From what I hear, women in the Autonomous Region retire at 55, while the men retire at 60. “Most of us are grandmothers by the time we are 50 and by then we are looking forward to retirement, which allows us quality time with our grandchildren, and pension, which comes a day or so before the start of a new month. It is good money for doing no work,” she winks before taking out her phone and showing me a picture of her daughter, Jamila, looking smart in an Emirates airline stewardess’s uniform. Sunny also has a four-year-old grandson. Muslims also get to enjoy more holidays on their festivals and ceremonious days. “Where we get something like three days off from work, the others get only a day off,” Sunny smiles. Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

Babar advised rest after hand injury in tour match. LONDON: Pakistan Test captain Babar Azam was advised to take no further part in the team’s three-day practice match against the Professional County Club (PCC) Select XI on Friday after being struck on the right hand, the Pakistan Cricket Board said. According to the PCB, Babar was hit while batting on the second day of the match at the Kent County Cricket Ground, Beckenham. Following an assessment by the team doctor, he was advised to rest for the remainder of the fixture as a precautionary measure. The PCB said Babar would participate in Pakistan’s practice session at Headingley Cricket Ground on Monday, two days before the first Test against England begins at the same venue. The development came as Pakistan were bowled out for 238 in their first innings on the second day, having resumed at 44 without loss in reply to the PCC Select XI’s 305. Pakistan’s innings followed a strong opening day for the hosts, who were dismissed for 305 despite four half-centuries, with Saif Zaib top-scoring with 65, Matt Fisher remaining unbeaten on 62, Caleb Falconer making 59 and Tom Haines scoring 51. Mohammad Ali and Mohammad Abbas claimed three wickets apiece for Pakistan, with Ali finishing with three for 23 and Abbas three for 37. England opener Emilio Gay fell for a duck early in the innings, edging Abbas to Salman Ali Agha in the third over after Pakistan had appealed off the first delivery of the match. Abbas then had James Rew caught behind for four before Haines launched an aggressive counterattack, reaching his half-century from only 30 balls, including 12 fours. He was eventually trapped lbw by Ali. Falconer and Zaib then put on 110, though both benefited from dropped chances. Falconer, on 29, edged Ubaid Shah but was dropped by Abdullah Shafique at first slip, while Zaib survived a stumping opportunity against Sajid Khan. Zaib eventually fell for 65 while attempting to hook Khurram Shahzad, with Awais Zafar taking a difficult catch on the boundary. Falconer was subsequently caught behind off Abbas for 59. Ali struck twice in quick succession later in the innings, removing Luc Benkenstein and Noah Thain, while Aamer Jamal dismissed Charlie Tear. Fisher and James Sales added 55 before Sales edged Ali Usman to Saud Shakeel. Speaking after the first day, Ali said the pitch offered sufficient assistance to fast bowlers despite not having the lush-green appearance that had been discussed before the match. “I think the pitch was very good for fast bowling,” Ali said. “If you bowl consistently in good areas, I still feel there is enough assistance for the fast bowlers.” He acknowledged Pakistan had allowed Fisher to score too freely but felt the bowling effort had otherwise been encouraging. “During the period when we conceded around 50 runs to Matt Fisher, we did not bowl particularly well. Apart from that, throughout the day we bowled very well,” he said. Ali also underlined the value of the match in preparing for England’s conditions, which he said differed from those Pakistan had encountered in the West Indies. “Here, you have to pitch the ball a little fuller to get the maximum results and take enough wickets,” he said, describing the three-day fixture as “ideal preparation” for the Test series. Pakistan’s first innings of 238 leaves them 67 runs behind the PCC Select XI, with play continuing on Friday. The Beckenham fixture was originally scheduled as a four-day game but was reduced to three days because of player availability, with it agreed that all 14 members of Pakistan’s Test squad could participate. The opening Test against England starts at Headingley on Aug 19, followed by Tests at Lord’s and The Oval. Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

Trump signals plan to claim Hormuz ‘soon’. • Urges Americans to accept higher gas prices to stop Iran going nuclear • UAE accuses Tehran of attacking two vessels; shipping in the strait comes to near standstill • Riyadh, Abu Dhabi, Doha condemn strikes, demand unconditional return to free navigation • Houthis strike Saudi oil site, Yemen’s Mocha port; eight killed • JD Vance confirms keeping US energy prices down is ‘goal number one’; Bessent vows sanctions ‘world has never seen’ against Tehran GARDEN CITY: US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he would “soon” declare the strategic Strait of Hormuz a US territory once Iran is defeated, even as fresh attacks on Emirati oil tankers brought maritime traffic in the vital waterway to a near standstill. Trump’s remarks at a New York rally underscored the escalating international struggle over the narrow corridor, where a grinding stalemate of retaliatory blockades has shifted Washington’s immediate wartime focus from containing Iran’s nuclear programme to preventing an energy crisis that could hit Americans at the pump. “After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated — pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States,” Trump said with a chuckle during an appearance at a police academy in New York state. “It’s true.” “We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to,” Trump told a cheering crowd of supporters and police. He urged Americans to accept slightly higher gasoline prices as the cost of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Trump said Americans who had to “pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline” should remember that this was the cost of ensuring “a very evil country” could not have a nuclear weapon. “What we’re doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves … and we’re really doing a great job,” said Trump, adding he would never apologise for attacking Iran. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates accused Iran on Friday of attacking two state-owned commercial vessels transiting the strategic waterway. The UAE foreign ministry condemned what it described as a “hostile Iranian attack” on two vessels affiliated with the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), saying there were no injuries. ADNOC confirmed the vessels had been attacked on Thursday evening but said the incidents had been brought under control, according to the state news agency WAM . Britain’s United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations later reported two nearly identical drone strikes on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing minor damage. The incidents came just days after ADNOC said three of its tankers had also been attacked in the same waterway. The latest attacks appeared to have an immediate impact on shipping. Vessel-tracking data from Kpler suggested traffic through the strait had slowed dramatically on Friday, with only two non-oil vessels passing through and no crude shipments visible. With commercial transit severely disrupted, the United States vowed to maintain an indefinite naval blockade of Iranian ports and unleash historic economic pressure on Tehran. “Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we’ll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we’ll continue to,” US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters during a trip to Panama. Iran, meanwhile, has sought to use the strait as its strongest bargaining chip. By disrupting commercial shipping and threatening global oil supplies, Tehran has shifted the conflict from the battlefield to the world’s energy markets. “Alongside the threat to energy infrastructure in the region, Iran’s ability to restrict shipping through the strait is its main source of leverage in negotiations,” said Torbjorn Solvedt, principal Middle East analyst with risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft. That leverage was reflected in unusually candid remarks from Vice-President JD Vance, who acknowledged that keeping fuel prices low had overtaken Iran’s nuclear ambitions as Washington’s most immediate concern. “I know that oil is down today and it’s way down from the highs in the early days of the conflict,” Vance said on Fox News . “That’s goal number one — keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country. And then obviously goal number two is ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon.” Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the United States planned to inflict more financial damage on Iran, threatening to subject Tehran to economic isolation “like the world has never seen before”. “Watch this space for more announcements next week because we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation of a country,” he said in an interview. The remarks underscored how dramatically the conflict has evolved. What began as a campaign centred on preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon — consistently touted by President Donald Trump as his main reason for the war — has become a struggle over control of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow maritime corridor through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil supply normally passes. Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait, frequently attacking commercial ships, and wants to charge users for passage, which the US fiercely opposes. The US military reportedly burnt through stockpiles of costly high-tech missiles and other weapons in the months since the war started at a cost of billions and is now reportedly running low, limiting Trump’s options for resuming attacks on Iran. Meanwhile, Trump struggles to find a way out of the war and shies away from resuming large-scale attacks. The 80-year-old president’s approval rating is plummeting, the war is unpopular among Americans, and midterm elections are approaching in November. Republicans fear Trump and the war, which has caused gasoline prices to soar, will cost them their control of Congress. Only days ago Trump had said an agreement to reopen the strait was imminent. Now his administration seems to be digging in, with diplomacy on hold as he hopes economic suffering will cause Iran to yield. Regional powers condemned the latest attacks. Saudi Arabia denounced the targeting of two oil tankers belonging to the United Arab Emirates’ Abu Dhabi National Oil Company in the Strait of Hormuz. In a statement, Riyadh’s foreign ministry said the attacks constitute “an unacceptable recurrence of Iranian attacks targeting commercial vessels and tankers”. “The kingdom holds Iran fully responsible for the consequences of persisting in these attacks, demanding an immediate halt to these violations and adherence to relevant international laws,” the statement added. Qatar also strongly condemned an “Iranian attack” targeting two Emirati oil tankers belonging to ADNOC which were crossing the Strait of Hormuz, deeming it “a severe violation of international law, the freedom of maritime navigation, and a clear violation of UN Security Council resolution 2817”. In a statement, the foreign ministry reiterated Doha’s “firm rejection of using the Strait of Hormuz as leverage”, demanding that it be opened unconditionally. The regional conflict showed little sign of easing elsewhere. In Yemen, the country’s internationally recognised government said the Houthis fired six ballistic missiles at the Red Sea port of Mocha on Friday, killing eight people in an attack it said targeted civilian infrastructure and national assets. The Houthis, for their part, said they had targeted what they described as Saudi-backed military build-ups, weapons depots and warships belonging to Saudi-backed forces and “mercenaries” in Mocha with a barrage of ballistic missiles, claiming to have destroyed boats and military equipment. The group also said it had carried out a separate cross-border attack. The Houthi-run SABA news agency quoted a military source as saying the rebels had targeted an Aramco facility in the Saudi city of Najran with a drone. The source said the strike was in response to what it described as Saudi military aircraft entering airspace over the northeastern part of Yemen’s Saada governorate. It did not identify the specific facility targeted or say whether it had been hit. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities or Aramco. Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

An increase of 7-8 per cent is expected next week,” Mr Ashraf said. Meanwhile, the Pakistan Transport Council, a constituent of the All Pakistan Goods Transporters Alliance, announced that it had called off the nationwide strike following what it described as successful negotiations with the government. The council leadership said goods transportation operations from Karachi Port and Port Qasim were also being restored with immediate effect. They said a special committee formed by the prime minister and headed by Communications Minister Abdul Aleem Khan had held negotiations with the transporters. As a result, eight of the transporters’ immediate demands had been accepted, while committees had been constituted to address the remaining issues. The council said the agreement with the government carried the signatures of office-bearers representing 15 goods transport associations from across the country. Among their demands were no increase in toll taxes for one year, removal of additional toll plazas and implementation of a modern automated system. The council leadership also said an agreement had been reached for the immediate release, against bank guarantees, of vehicles detained under SRO 1619. The committees established to address other long-standing issues would remain in contact with the relevant government institutions, they added. He said the strike, which had continued for the past six days, was adversely affecting port activities. “The smaller goods carrier vehicles have called off the strike, but the large vehicles that move between provinces and carry heavy loads are still off the roads,” Mr Choudhry said. “The government is playing politics with us — buying time under the garb of negotiations while threatening our members through other means,” he alleged. Edible oil tankers also remained on strike. Edible Oil Contractors Association President Tariq Sarbaz said operators were not lifting palm oil and palm olein from the ports for transportation to oil factories. New administrative units ‘under serious consideration’. • Top govt functionary thinks discussion could be precursor to proposed 28th Constitutional Amendment • Proposals include bringing Karachi, Gwadar under federal control; splitting Punjab into three, KP into two units ISLAMABAD: There is a serious debate underway in power corridors over the most feasible approach to creating new provinces, according to a top government functionary, who thinks the discussion is a precursor to the proposed 28th Constitutional Amendment . The government source, who is privy to developments, was reluctant to say when the proposal — still said to be in the initial stages — could materialise. He conceded, however, that turning the idea of new administrative into reality would not be easy, as building a consensus among major political parties, which appear opposed to the idea, would be a major challenge. The functionary said discussions were focused on whether new provinces should be created and, if so, how many would suffice; whether more administrative units should instead be established; or whether the local government system should be revived and empowered. According to the source, the most effective way to address the consequences of the 18th Amendment was to create new provinces. He said this could help resolve many of the problems faced by the federal government following the devolution of powers to the provinces. Recently, while addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi urged all political parties to resolve key national issues, including the creation of new provinces, describing it as the only solution to improving the country’s overall condition, which he said had “collapsed”. The issue gained momentum after the minister’s proposal drew strong reactions from government ministers, while the country’s leading lawyers’ bodies adopted divergent positions . The Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) backed the proposal, whereas the Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) stressed that any such move must be pursued strictly within the constitutional fram­ework, through parliament and with national consensus. Speaking at a Full Court Reference held at the Supreme Court in honour of Justice Musarrat Hilali on her retirement, SCBA President Haroonur Rashid said the association endorsed and supported the proposal to create new provinces. He said the SCBA believed that any constitutional measure to create additional provinces would promote better governance through devolution and equitable administration at the grassroots level, create equal opportunities for balanced economic development and strengthen political stability. The creation of more provinces, he added, would also help improve living standards by addressing the economic hardships faced by people. The PBC, the apex representative body of the legal fraternity, meanwhile, said at its 250th meeting that all constitutional matters must be addressed strictly within the framework of the Constitution. How many more? The government functionary said that if it was ultimately decided that creating more provinces was the only solution to what the interior minister had described as a “collapsing system”, the next question would be how many provinces should be created. Under one proposal being discussed, he said, Karachi and Gwadar could come under the administrative control of the federal government, while the rest of Sindh would remain a single province. Similarly, Balochistan could be divided into two provinces, while Punjab could be divided into three. Khyber Pakhtun­khwa, however, presents a more complicated case beca­use of the merger of the erstwhile Federally Administered Tribal Areas (Fata) and the inco­rporation of areas previously administered under the Fata and Pata arrangements into the provincial constitutional, legal and judicial framework. The source said KP could nevertheless be divided into Pakhtun and Hazara regions. Stronger local govt Alternatively, he said, if the decision was taken to strengthen the local government system, funds for local governments could be channelled directly through the federal government instead of the provinces. Had the local government system introduced during the late President Pervez Musharraf’s tenure continued uninterrupted, he said, a large pool of experienced and competent councillors would have been available to address local issues effectively. “Unfortunately, reaching that level of experience and building such a team will now take considerable time,” he added. Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

Govt raises petroleum dealers’ margin to Rs9.98 per litre. • PPDA calls off nationwide strike planned from today • Higher margin to take effect from Sept 1 ISLAMABAD: In a move aimed at averting a nationwide strike by petroleum dealers, the Economic Coordination Com­mittee (ECC) of the federal cabinet on Friday approved a 15.5 per cent increase in dealers’ margins on both petrol and high-speed diesel, following which the dealers called off their protest planned from Saturday. The decision raises the dealers’ margin on both fuels by Rs1.34 per litre, from Rs8.64 to Rs9.98 per litre. The revised margin is scheduled to take effect from Sept 1. Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb chaired the ECC meeting virtually, while Finance Secretary Imdadullah Bosal attended in person at the Finance Division. The meeting was convened on a public holiday after petroleum dealers announced a nationwide strike from Aug 15, prompting the government to take up the matter on an urgent basis. The Finance Division’s statement did not disclose the exact increase in dealers’ margins. However, officials confirmed that the ECC had approved the proposal submitted by the Petroleum Division. “Yes, the ECC approved the same increase proposed by the Petroleum Division,” a senior official privy to the meeting told Dawn . According to the summary submitted to the ECC, the dealers’ margin was proposed to be increased by Rs1.34 per litre to Rs9.98. Soon after the decision, the Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) called off its plan to launch a nationwide strike from Saturday. The association had earlier given the federal government a 72-hour ultimatum , accusing it of failing to honour assurances made by the petroleum minister regarding its demands. The dealers had sought replacement of the existing fixed margin with a variable margin linked to the retail prices of petrol and diesel, proposing that it be set at 8pc of the retail price of both fuels. According to official sources, acceptance of that demand would have raised the dealers’ margin to around Rs26 per litre on petrol and Rs30 per litre on diesel at current retail prices, resulting in a substantially higher burden on consumers. The ECC instead approved the 15.51pc increase in the fixed margin. The margin of oil marketing companies (OMCs) remains unchanged at Rs7.87 per litre on both petrol and diesel. A proposal to increase the OMC margin by Rs1.22 per litre remains linked to the implementation of digitisation measures. An official Finance Division statement said the ECC considered a summary submitted by the Petroleum Division and deliberated on the revision of dealers’ margins on motor spirit and high-speed diesel (HSD). In December 2025, the ECC had approved an increase of Rs2.56 per litre in dealers’ margins on petrol and diesel. The decision was subsequently modified by the federal cabinet, prompting the PPDA to demand its implementation. The shift from fortnightly to daily petroleum price revisions added another demand from dealers, who sought to link their margins to retail prices. The government, however, decided to retain the daily pricing mechanism. Under the ECC’s December 2025 decision, 50pc of the proposed increase was to take effect from Dec 15, subject to a declining trend in petroleum prices, while the remaining 50pc was linked to achievement of digitisation targets set by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). On Dec 23, the federal cabinet modified the decision, making the increase conditional on completion of digitisation targets by OMCs and petroleum dealers. With the digitisation drive still under way, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik held a meeting on July 22 with representatives of the All Pakistan Petrol Pump Owners Association and the PPDA following an earlier strike call. Senior Petroleum Division officials and the Ogra chairman also attended. The dealers urged the government to delink the increase in their margins from digitisation, arguing that implementation of the initiative was primarily the responsibility of OMCs. They also reiterated their demand that the fixed margin of Rs8.64 per litre be replaced with a margin equivalent to 8pc of the retail price of petrol and diesel. Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

The Jhelum at Mangla recorded inflows of 28,400 cusecs and outflows of 7,000 cusecs, while the Chenab at Marala had inflows of 81,000 cusecs and outflows of 62,000 cusecs. The Middle East’s Nato?. ON Aug 7, 2026, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye signed the historic Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA) to strengthen collective deterrence against external armed aggression. The agreement provides that an armed attack on one state would be regarded as an attack on all parties to the agreement. Historically, Pakistan has maintained long-standing defence ties with both countries. For example, Turkiye has supplied corvettes to Pakistan, while Pakistan has supplied training aircraft to Turkiye; Saudi Arabia, too, has purchased Turkish drones. Pakistan has also provided training and technical assistance to Saudi forces. Previously, Pakistan has entered into defence and military cooperation agreements with Saudi Arabia as well as other GCC countries. MJDA is grounded in international law. Article 51 of the United Nations Charter recognises the inherent right to individual or collective self-defence when an armed attack occurs against a member state. Article 51, located in Chapter VII of the UN Charter, is the principal exception to the general prohibition on the threat or use of force in international relations established under Article 2(4) of the Charter, which protects the territorial integrity and political independence of states. Crucially, self-defence is triggered only by an “armed attack” establishing a high threshold for the lawful use of force. In practice, states have used force in self-defence both after an armed attack and, more controversially, on a pre-emptive or anticipatory basis. Such force has been used unilaterally as well as collectively with allies. A prominent example of collective self-defence followed the Sept 11, 2001, attacks, when Nato invoked Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty for the first time. Article 5 provides that an armed attack against one or more Nato members is considered an attack against all, requiring each member to assist the state attacked, including through armed force where deemed necessary. Controversial claims of collective self-defence have also arisen where a state has used force against another state purportedly in defence of a third state, in the absence of a mutual defence arrangement. One such case arose when the US used force against Nicaragua, claiming collective self-defence of El Salvador, alleging that Nicaragua was arming and assisting Salvadoran rebels fighting its government. The dispute ultimately came before the International Court of Justice in Military and Paramilitary Activities in and against Nicaragua. The right to collective self-defence has, in practice, been invoked not only against other UN member states, but also against internal threats, or what has been interpreted as armed attacks attributed to terrorist groups and other non-state actors. Examples where states have requested foreign assistance as collective self-defence or, at a minimum, intervention by consent against internal threats, include the Syrian request for Russian assistance, and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government’s request from Saudi Arabia and its allies against the Houthis, the latter expressly invoking Article 51 of the UN Charter. The Iraqi government also requested armed assistance against IS, providing the basis for states to invoke collective self-defence of Iraq against an international terrorist group. Iraq maintained that IS posed a serious threat to its people and territorial sovereignty. Moreover, the UN Security Council recognised IS as a threat to international peace and security. The new trilateral security agreement raises questions about its costs for Pakistan. Regarding global terrorism, the UN Security Council had earlier, somewhat controversially, recognised this position. Resolution 1368 (2001), adopted the day after 9/11, affirmed the inherent right of individual and collective self-defence in the context of those attacks. Resolution 1373 (2001) reaffirmed this right while strengthening global counterterrorism obligations. The US subsequently used force in Afghanistan under Article 51, while Nato separately invoked Article 5 of its collective defence pact. Geopolitically, notwithstanding the potential benefits — including greater economic assistance from Saudi Arabia and other GCC states, and likely US support — the agreement raises questions about its costs for Pakistan and, more importantly, what Pakistan can realistically provide. Pakistan has consistently maintained that such arrangements would not extend its nuclear umbrella. Practically, questions arise over how Pakistan could protect Turkish security interests, whether against Israel or internal threats from Kurdish separatist groups operating from Syria and Iraq. Regarding Saudi Arabia, reciprocal security guarantees may exist in theory, but their practical operation remains unclear. It is uncertain what meaningful military assistance Saudi Arabia could provide Pakistan in a conflict with India, with which it maintains close ties. More broadly, it is unclear what security benefits Pakistan would receive in return. The agreement could also draw Pakistan into a more direct confrontation with Israel, which has long maintained close defence ties with India and could further strengthen them in response. The agreement also risks placing Pakistan at odds with Iran, with which it shares a long border and has at times cooperated against cross-border security threats. Involvement in a conflict with Iran over Middle Eastern security could further destabilise Pakistan’s western frontier while relations with Afghanistan and India remain tense and conflict-ridden. Pakistan has accused both states of facilitating terrorism and undermining its security. Moreover, Pakistan has the world’s second-largest Shia population after Iran. Any conflict with Iran could potentially strain internal cohesion and intensify sectarian tensions that Pakistan already struggles to contain. Finally, if Pakistan is willing to enter mutual-defence pacts, why not prioritise one with China, which has major economic interests in Pakistan through CPEC and a strong stake in safeguarding this country’s external security? Such an arrangement could be mutually beneficial and deter further Indian adventurism, particularly given the effectiveness of the Pakistan-China defence cooperation and China-origin military systems during the four-day May 2025 Pakistan-India clash . Historically, Western states have acquiesced in Pakistan’s possession and maintenance of nuclear weapons, largely in the context of its rivalry with India and stated self-defence needs. However, deeper integration into Middle Eastern and broader global security frameworks could generate greater Western pressure, including through international institutions, to constrain Pakistan’s nuclear weapons, missile technology and ballistic programmes. Such pressure could directly threaten Pakistan’s sovereignty and security. Lastly, the agreement could draw Pakistan’s armed forces into conflicts in which the country has historically maintained neutrality. Such commitments could stretch military resources, create fatigue, and increase vulnerability to Indian or Afghan opportunism and adventurism. The writer is a professor of law at Lums. Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

Death in Karachi. ON the night of Aug 13, 2026, Mir Raza Ali’s father was on TV imploring — as he had been doing for some time — for justice. It is now over two weeks since Mir Raza Ali, a 25-year-old businessman, left his home on an ill-fated trip that would be his last. The gruesome nature of his death, questions surrounding the initial police investigation and the inconsistent behaviour of the officials demonstrate why parents in Karachi so fear their children leaving their homes. In this sense, there are at least three dimensions to the death of Mir Raza Ali. First is the immense grief and the individual tragedy faced by the family of the young man. The death of one so young is heartbreaking enough, but the horrific details of this case and the mystery that surrounds those who appeared to have tortured and killed him have deepened the tragedy. Second is the story of lapses in the investigation of his death and the dismissive attitude of Karachi’s police force towards the violent deaths of young people. Third, there is the message that the ongoing disclosures and delays convey to the people of an exhausted and neglected city. The violent death of Mir Raza Ali has gripped the city. Here was a young man who did not leave the country despite having the opportunity to do so. Mir Raza was a business wunderkind, starting a business on next to nothing as an 18-year-old and making it a resounding success. In interviews, Mir Raza leveraged this fact as evidence that there is hope for the young in Karachi and the rest of the country. He created jobs for scores of people. One of them, holding a placard at Karachi’s Teen Talwar area, could not stop his tears when talking about just how well-mannered, professional and respectful the young man had been. If the family had not been able to somehow set up a protest movement — and Karachi’s police surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed had not been so blunt in noting deficiencies in the initial postmortem — Mir Raza Ali’s death might have continued to be treated as possible suicide. The second postmortem found multiple injuries, including fractures and a wound caused by a bullet entering from the back; a murder charge was subsequently added. We now come to the second dimension of the case: the lapses and negligence that have so far come to light. As such failures are uncovered, they underscore the impunity with which the institutional structure can frustrate efforts at investigating homicide in the city. A judicial commission was proposed but deferred after the family expressed confidence in a new police investigation team. The level of protection available to officials who fail in their duties seems to be so formidable that few appear bothered enough to even provide convincing justifications for their actions. This situation reflects a collapse of the administrative system and a hollowing out of democratic institutions to say the least. No one is more alone than a victim of crime in Karachi. The third and most pernicious aspect is the message that this case and others like it send to those living in the city. Karachi denizens are used to living life in defensive mode. On the surface, things seem to function. Drive around the city at night and restaurants are full, people are shopping, traffic is everywhere — but life is merely a thread away from being extinguished. No one is more alone than a citizen of Karachi who has become a victim of crime. If your home is robbed, your child is missing or your money is stolen, you are immediately alone. The idea of justice has become anathema. Even if you want an FIR registered for a robbery, you may have to bribe the police; it follows that when som­eone is killed, few believe justice will be brought to the perpetrators. This latest case just substantiates the feeling of futility and resignation that casts its shadow over millions of people. Changing medical boards, changing hypotheses of the case, changing investigation officials, selectively releasing information, officials saying one thing and then nothing — all show how unsafe and broken this city has become. Investigative teams, medical boards, postmortem reports, DNA and toxicology findings imply that the data gathered will hopefully lead to some conclusion, and perhaps closure. But the point is that, all too often, there is no point at all. The powerful and indifferent wait it out until the blood dries on the ground and there are new murders to ignore or pass off as suicides. Perhaps the definition of being suicidal in Karachi is simply staying in the city. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy. rafia.zakaria@gmail.com Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

Governance test. EVER since the interior minister called for smaller administrative units to improve governance, the question of new provinces has become the subject of much discussion. The proposal has revived a long-standing debate: does Pakistan need more provinces or greater devolution to the local level? A recent discussion in Islamabad on the topic brought together politicians, policymakers, technocrats and civil society representatives. While some participants supported the creation of new provinces, the broader sentiment appeared to favour, and rightly so, the decentralisation of political, administrative and financial power through effective local governments. The case for smaller provinces rests on the view that large administrative units have become unwieldy due to racing population numbers and the concentration of authority in a few urban centres. Proponents of this view argue that smaller provinces will bring governance closer to citizens and address the challenges. Yet even they recognise that any restructuring must reflect the will of the people and follow the constitutional process. This is vital to ensure that boundary changes do not become an exercise in political engineering, but emerge from genuine public demand. However, Pakistan’s problem is less a shortage of provinces than excessive centralisation of every kind of power. Without empowered LGs and devolved resources, creating new provinces will not improve governance. The more immediate task should be to make LGs genuinely functional. After all, citizens turn most often to elected representatives over basic issues such as roads, streets, sewerage and other necessary municipal services. These are the challenges that should be addressed at the local level. Sadly, because of the political ambitions of the ruling elite, LGs in Pakistan have intentionally been denied adequate administrative and financial powers. The outcome is a distorted structure in which provincial governments perform functions that should be handled much closer to the citizens. This results in political patronage, administrative congestion and poor service delivery. The debate therefore rightly widened the reform agenda. Judicial and electoral reforms, intra-party democracy, the rule of law and institutional behaviour cannot be separated from the question of good governance. As some participants noted, changing boundaries without reforming the underlying political and institutional culture will only lead to the same governance failures. New provinces may, where there is genuine public demand and a sound administrative and fiscal case, form part of a broader governance restructuring. But the first test is whether power is actually transferred to the citizens. We need governments that are closer to the people, more accountable and financially empowered. The aim should not be to redraw Pakistan’s map. It should be to redraw the relationship between the state and its citizens. Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

Date workers toil through rising heat in Sindh. KHAIRPUR: In blazing temperatures, Muhammad Idrees ladles boiled dates from a vat simmering over an open flame, work that labourers lament is getting hotter each year in Sindh. Date season arrives in July, when temperatures in the province regularly hit the mid-40 degrees Celsius. Workers start before sunrise, and split the day into short shifts, but the heat soon catches up with them. Their gruelling routine involves harvesting and boiling fruit picked from palms that line Khairpur district, which produces more than half the country’s dates and supports thousands of farmers and seasonal labourers. Labourers begin work around 2am to avoid the worst of the daytime heat Idrees, who has worked the date harvest for more than a decade, said the heat has now become “unbearable”. Date labourers are one of many professions in Pakistan that are becoming more difficult and dangerous as temperatures rise. “It used to be less intense,” Idrees told AFP as temperatures hit 42°C. “The heat is much harsher and the days are extremely hot. We fall ill because of it.” Multiple workers said they often suffer heatstroke, fainting and fever. “When the heat makes us sick, we go to the doctor for treatment and then return to work,” Idrees added. Pakistan is among the countries globally most vulnerable to climate change despite contributing less than one per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions. The country has experienced increasingly frequent heatwaves, erratic monsoon rains and devastating floods, including catastrophic 2022 floods that inundated around one-third of the country and displaced millions, hitting Sindh particularly hard. Heat and harvest Workers descend on date farms to begin work around 2am to avoid the worst of the daytime heat and take a break before continuing until the late evening. Idrees said the physically demanding work earns him around Rs1,200, roughly $4, a day. “We harvest the dates, load them onto trolleys and bring them here,” he said. “They are boiled over the fire and then spread outside in the sun to dry.” Pakistan, the world’s fifth-largest date producer, normally earns more than $120 million a year in exports, according to industry estimates. Date farmer Shahnawaz Phulpoto, who owns more than 1,500 palm trees, said that heavy monsoon rains from shifting weather patterns have hampered date crops and caused financial losses. But for now the main challenge is the heat, he added, as the sun blazed overhead. “The temperature rises every year,” he said, adding: “We are seeing the effects of climate change every year.” Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

Powerful quake off Indonesia kills 20, sparks mass evacuations. Rescuers combed through debris for survivors on Saturday after a powerful earthquake struck off Flores island in eastern Indonesia, killing at least 20 people and sending thousands fleeing. As the full scale of the disaster unfolded, rescue official Fathur Rahman told AFP at least 20 people were confirmed dead from four different towns on the island, popular with tourists. “From the reports we have received, 20 people have died, six are injured, and two are still buried,” Fathur said by telephone from a boat on his way to Nagekeo regency, the hardest-hit area. Two people were known to be trapped alive under rubble in the neighbouring Manggarai regency after the 7.7-magnitude jolt. “Our focus will be on locating the victims who are buried under the rubble” said Fathur, adding the rescue effort had been complicated by landslides cutting off several roads. Residents in Nagekeo, the area closest to the epicentre, raced for higher ground as the sea retreated earlier Saturday — a possible sign of an approaching tsunami, AFP journalists witnessed. A tsunami warning was later lifted but people were warned not to return to damaged buildings for fear that aftershocks may bring them down. Dozens of aftershocks have already been felt, the strongest measured at a magnitude of 6.1. ‘My family is safe’ Yohanes Babo, 56, a resident of Nagekeo, said he was at a market when the earth started shaking in the early morning hours. “The shaking was strong. Thankfully, we were already outside the house,” he told AFP . “People were panicking, running here and there. We’re evacuating for the time being … and trying to get to the hills,” he said, adding: “My family is safe. No one was harmed.” The epicentre of the shallow quake was located just off the north coast of the island, about 68 kilometres (42 miles) northwest of the coastal town of Ende, US and Indonesian authorities said. Rescuers pull one dead body from the rubble of a building that partly collapsed at the port of Maumere. Fathur said two people were evacuated alive from the debris and “one was found deceased”, according to video footage released by the agency. The full extent of the damage is still being assessed. Lukas Lotar, a resident of Maumere about 2,500 kilometres (1,553 miles) east of Jakarta, recounted how the earth “suddenly started to shake and I panicked”. “Patients also fled the hospital, the jolt was big. I saw some walls were cracked,” Lotar, a hospital customer service official told AFP . The stricken area is comprised mostly of towns and villages with few, if any, high-rise buildings. Monitoring sea level Indonesia’s Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) initially warned of possible tsunami waves following the quake and urged people to get to higher ground. Long queues of people could be seen evacuating towns on foot, by motorbike and car, some piled into the back of pickup trucks. “We have ended (the tsunami warning) but we will keep monitoring the sea level,” said BMKG earthquake and tsunami director Wijayanto, who like many Indonesians goes by one name. Indonesia and neighbouring countries experience frequent earthquakes due to their location in the Pacific “Ring of Fire” — an arc of intense seismic activity stretching from Japan through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific basin. Flores was struck by a 7.7-magnitude earthquake in 1992, which triggered a tsunami and resulted in around 2,500 deaths. Among Indonesia’s history of deadly quakes is a devastating 9.1-magnitude tremor in 2004 that struck off the coast of Sumatra and triggered a tsunami that killed 220,000 throughout the region, about 170,000 of them in Indonesia. The Boxing Day tragedy was one of the deadliest natural disasters in recorded history. In 2018, a powerful quake shook the island of Lombok and several more tremors followed over the next couple of weeks, killing more than 550 people on the holiday island and neighbouring Sumbawa. Later that year, a 7.5-magnitude quake and a subsequent tsunami in Palu on Sulawesi island left more than 4,300 people dead or missing.

Ex-Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism scandal found dead. Black academic Jason Arday, who resigned from the University of Cambridge last week following a high-profile plagiarism scandal that raised claims of racism, was found dead on Friday, the prestigious British institution confirmed. Arday, 41, was found unresponsive Friday afternoon at an address in south London, according to the capital’s Metropolitan Police Service, which did not confirm the identity of the deceased person at the time of discovery. “We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news,” Cambridge University’s top administrator, Vice Chancellor Deborah Prentice, said in a brief statement. Arday’s family criticised what they called a “campaign of harassment” that followed allegations about his academic work and personal life. “The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone,” the family said in a statement released through his publisher Simon & Schuster. The scandal erupted after some academics and media reports accused Arday, who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, of plagiarising parts of his doctoral thesis. The allegations have been seized on by British right-wing newspapers and commentators, who claim that he unfairly benefited from diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies. Arday announced on August 5 that he was resigning from both his university post as a professor and as a fellow of Jesus College, shortly after they announced probes into the various accusations. In a letter posted online, Arday said that quitting was “the only way” to end a “difficult period”, but insisted the decision should not be “mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me”. Newspaper claims Police said officers had been called by the London Ambulance Service “following a report that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property” in the city’s Battersea neighbourhood. “Sadly, a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene,” it said in a statement, noting his next-of-kin had been informed. “At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious. “The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s Central South Command Unit. A file will be prepared for the coroner.” Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was “deeply shocked (and) saddened” by the news. She urged people to give his family “privacy through this incredibly difficult period (and) to remember there are real people with loved ones involved”. The furore around Arday grew after Nathan Cofnas, a US academic and self-defined “race realist” — whose Cambridge research affiliation ended in 2024 amid racism accusations — published claims about him in July. The allegations included that multiple sections of Arday’s doctoral dissertation were copied from other works. The Times and Telegraph newspapers have published several investigative articles into Arday’s academic work and personal life. Some of his claims about his personal life, including that he once ran 30 marathons in 35 days and raised millions for charities, were also disputed. ‘Racially motivated’ In an interview with The Times earlier this month, Arday admitted making academic “mistakes” but said he was being wrongly “portrayed to be a liar and a fantasist and an academic fraud”. He also alleged the “campaign to unseat me from my position” was “racially motivated”. The controversy around Arday appears to have divided the Cambridge campus and wider academia. A group of university academics last week wrote to Prentice slamming Arday’s appointment and asking her to appoint an independent body to probe what happened. Others have written joint letters in support of him. On Wednesday, Prentice had called his alleged wrongdoing “an aberration” and vowed a thorough and transparent investigation, while insisting it should not be used “to cast aspersions” on other academics from ethnic minority backgrounds. The American psychologist promised the probe would look into the “circumstances” of Arday’s appointment and his time in post that would include academics from “beyond Cambridge”. Arday’s memoir — Great and Unfortunate Things — had been published in the United States the previous day, ahead of its planned release in Britain later this month. It has also attracted scrutiny.

Balloting underway at 23 polling stations in 2 constituencies of AJK's Bagh district. Polling is currently underway at 23 stations in two constituencies of Azad Jammu and Kashmir’s Bagh district. Polling began at 8am and will continue till 5pm. In the third phase of polling on Monday, PPP’s Sardar Ziaul Qamar secured 16,637 votes in LA-15 (Bagh Central), followed by PML-N’s Mushtaq Ahmed Minhas with 15,015 and Jamaat-i-Islami’s retired Brig Dr Muhammad Khan with 12,259. But as polling could not be held at nine stations in the constituency, the commission withheld the result. Similarly, the result of LA-16 (Eastern Bagh) was also withheld after polling could not be held at 14 stations, which have a combined 7,238 registered voters. Results from the remaining polling stations showed that PML-N’s Sardar Mir Akbar, who secured 19,515 votes, was leading his closest rival, PPP’s Sardar Qamaruz Zaman, by 3,225 votes. In both constituencies, all five candidates had accused their opponents of massive rigging. “Since we have more than enough police and other law enforcement personnel available, we have made adequate deployment at the polling stations to provide a fear-free environment to voters,” Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) retired Justice Ghulam Mustafa Mughal told Dawn on Saturday. The PML-N bagged 24 seats — nine from Mirpur division in the first phase on July 27 and 15 in the second phase on Aug 2 comprising Muzaffarabad Division and the 12 refugee seats. The PPP, on the other hand, won only 10 constituencies during these phases. The polls are being held in phases amid unrest in the region. The third phase, held on Monday, was originally meant to cover all of Poonch Division, which comprises 11 constituencies, including three in Bagh, one in Haveli, five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti district. However, the AJK Election Commission announced that polling would only go ahead as scheduled in Bagh and Haveli because of concerns over the law and order situation. On Monday, polls went ahead in Bagh and Haveli, but the Election Commission later withheld the results of two constituencies pending repolling at 23 polling stations. It announced the result for LA-14 (Bagh-I), commonly known as Dhirkot, where Jammu Kashmir Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party candidate Sajid Iqbal Abbasi secured a landslide victory with 40,522 votes. LA-17 (Haveli), where AJK Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore was contesting from, emerged as the most contentious constituency. The election was thrown into fresh controversy on Wednesday after the returning officer issued the Form 27 declaring him the winner despite an assurance, according to his PML-N rival Engr Mohsin Aziz, that the result would not be announced until his complaint was taken up by the Election Commission. Aziz subsequently challenged the election, with the AJK Chief Election Co­­mmissioner (CEC) retired Justice Ghulam Mustafa Mughal on Thursday reserving his decision after hearing arguments from both sides.
