Kelvin Morales translates aura, energy, and emotion into fashion. When we talk about aura, more often than not, people tend to say, “You have this certain glow.” Some pair it with other terms, say, confidence, power, relaxation, and joy. It is kind of hard to really identify its meaning. Merriam-Webster alone has a handful of definitions for it. But, for many, the easiest way to give meaning to aura is through colors. Whether viewed as a spiritual energy, a reflection of one’s personality, or simply a metaphor for the impression we leave on others, these colors have long been associated with different emotions, qualities, and energies. That’s exactly what Filipino fashion designer Kelvin Morales is trying to discover with his latest collection: the ever-changing energy that surrounds us. Aptly titled “Aura,” the line also marks his first foray into womenswear, with pieces that are unconventional yet still familiar. “About two years ago, I became really sensitive to people's energy. I started noticing what I interpreted as different aura colors around people. It honestly sounded strange even to me, so I got curious and started reading about what each color could mean,” Kelvin tells Manila Bulletin Lifestyle. “Surprisingly, a lot of it felt accurate based on the people around me. What fascinated me the most is that an aura isn't just one color—it shifts, blends, and changes.” It was in October last year when Kelvin started to conceive the collection. He used the aura colors he saw from the people who surrounded him as a guide for his process. And that is important. He wanted it to be intentional, rather than simply playing with trending hues or choosing colors based on what was popular at the time. In this way, the collection became more than an exercise in color; it became a visual interpretation of the human energy he encountered around him. The challenge now is how to reflect them through his garments. “I worked with a lot of sheer and textured fabrics because I wanted to show layers and transitions, almost like how an aura changes,” the designer muses. “I also played with different fabric depths, layering, and adjustable details so the pieces could transform depending on how they're worn.” Another unique perspective he is trying to convey with the collection is his take on womenswear. He asked himself the question: “If I were designing clothes for myself as a woman, what would I want?” The result is a play on contrast: delicate textiles are used for structured silhouettes, everyday pieces like denim and tops are paired with pieces featuring fabric manipulation, and minimalist whites serve as a canvas for decorative elements. “I found myself designing for someone who appreciates a more understated, tomboy-chic style,” Kelvin explains. “I'd want pieces that are versatile, easy to style, and something I could keep wearing for years. I didn't want clothes that only work for one occasion. I wanted them to adapt to different women and different lifestyles.” When designing a collection that is inspired by things the naked eye doesn’t usually see, one has to be more creative to fully imbibe its spirit. In Kelvin’s case, sound and scents helped. “I'm such a vibe person. I always need the right playlist and even the right scent whenever I'm designing a collection,” he confesses. “For ‘Aura,’ I kept listening to ‘Window’ by MC Yogi. It has this calm, uplifting energy that feels like sunlight recharging you. I also wore Blanche by Byredo because it's such a clean and pure scent. It reminds me of fresh laundry and clouds. Those little things really help me get into the creative mood.” According to Kelvin, talking about aura and energy is still a bit taboo for some people, but he realized that a lot of the people around him genuinely believe in auras, crystals, and energy as a form of guidance or protection. He thought it would be interesting to translate that into fashion. “I hope it opens people's minds a little more. Whether you believe in aura or not, I think it's interesting to realize that there are so many different ways of seeing the world,” Kelvin concludes.

Gov’t cutting discretionary powers to protect public funds — Marcos. President Marcos said his administration is reducing discretionary powers in government and expanding digitalization to strengthen safeguards in the management of public funds and prevent corruption and waste. Speaking at the traditional Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP) Presidential Luncheon in Manila, the President lamented that oversight mechanisms were not being properly observed or implemented. “Many of these oversight measures were actually in place. They were just not being respected or used,” the President said Friday, Aug. 14. Marcos said the administration had identified excessive discretion among government officials as an area requiring immediate attention after finding that decision-making authority had been delegated to lower levels of the bureaucracy. “And we noticed that discretion has become, has gone to a much lower, to a lower and lower part of the administration until rank-and-file members are making decisions that are in the billions of pesos,” he said. Such decisions, he noted, could enter a “very gray area” and, in some cases, could be “absolutely and totally illegal.” “So, that is one of the measures that we have put in: to remove that discretion,” Marcos said, adding that excessive discretionary authority was where “the corruption comes in.” According to the Chief Executive, unchecked discretion could allow government officials to demand money or enter into arrangements in exchange for decisions favoring certain individuals at the expense of the government. “If I, let us say, a functionary, can make big decisions, then I can ask for money and say, I will decide it in your favor if you give me money,” Marcos said. The President identified digitalization as the administration’s “most powerful tool” for reducing human intervention in government processes and limiting opportunities for corruption and waste. “Digitalization is our most powerful tool for that because we remove that human element where wastage and corruption can creep into,” he said. One of the administration’s initiatives is the use of blockchain technology for the 2026 national budget, which the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) said is intended to provide a permanent, tamper-proof digital record of the budget and eventually cover the entire budget cycle from approval and spending to disbursement and reporting. DICT Secretary Henry Aguda said in January that the blockchain system, called the Digital Bayanihan Chain, would serve as a “digital seal of truth” that would allow citizens, auditors, researchers, and future administrations to verify official budget records even years after they were created. Marcos had previously said blockchain could help address transparency problems in government spending, telling a podcast interviewer last year, “Blockchain is something that could work,” while also stressing that existing rules needed to be followed. The President has likewise tightened safeguards over the 2026 budget, including vetoing nearly P92.5 billion in Unprogrammed Appropriations and saying such funds should not be treated as a “backdoor for discretionary spending,” while requiring clearly defined triggers and careful validation before their release. Marcos said the administration would continue improving government processes to ensure that discretionary authority is not abused and that public spending and government projects are implemented more safely and equitably.

Marcos confident gov’t spending will surpass 2025 level by Q4. President Marcos expressed confidence that the government would catch up with and surpass last year’s level of public spending by the fourth quarter of 2026, with faster expenditures expected to support economic growth. Speaking at the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP) Presidential Luncheon in Manila on Friday, Aug. 14, the President said government spending had been delayed after the administration conducted a close review of the previous year’s national budget. “But again, in terms of public spending, we are pretty much on current, in terms of our scheduling,” he said. “I am confident we will be able to catch up and exceed the year-on-year public spending by the last quarter of this year,” he added. Marcos said projects under the National Expenditure Program (NEP) are normally bid out before the start of the fiscal year to allow their immediate implementation once the budget takes effect. The review of the previous year’s budget, however, resulted in some projects and contracts being bid out only toward the end of the first quarter of 2026, delaying government expenditures. “That is what happened. That's why it delayed the public spending,” Marcos said. According to the President, the administration subsequently adopted measures to accelerate government expenditures, narrowing the spending gap to about seven percent year-on-year by the end of the second quarter. “As of the end of the second quarter of this year, we are only at a shortfall of about 7 percent year on year in terms of public spending,” he said. “We will make that up for the rest of the year,” he added. Marcos said faster government spending was expected to increase economic activity and contribute to higher gross domestic product (GDP) growth. He, however, cautioned that accelerating spending should take into account the capacity of government agencies and private contractors to implement projects. “What we are running into very much is the absorptive capacity, not only of the government agencies, but also of the contractors,” the President said. “They can only do so much work,” he added. Marcos likewise stressed that simply increasing expenditures without considering implementation capacity would not necessarily improve project delivery. “So throwing money at the problem simply doesn't solve it, doesn't make anything better,” he said. “That is the balance that we are trying to manage right now,” he added. The administration has also used public spending for direct assistance and subsidies intended to cushion households from elevated food and fuel prices, including diesel subsidies and support for the transport sector. President Marcos cited lower tariffs on imported rice, the expansion of the P20-per-kilo rice program, and government assistance benefiting around 7.5 million Filipino families as part of efforts to ease inflationary pressures. He said restoring economic stability remained a priority amid external pressures, particularly higher global oil prices and uncertainty arising from the conflict in the Middle East. “We are hoping that the situation in the Strait of Hormuz improves,” Marcos said, noting that stable shipping routes would help provide more predictable conditions for petroleum supplies and economic planning.

Interest-free loan alternative Filipino buyers need to know about. For a long time, the prevailing narrative surrounding Islamic banking in the Philippines was trapped in a narrow frame. Most consumers assumed it was a niche service exclusive to Muslim communities or strictly intended for regional development in Mindanao. Amenah “Mina” Pangandaman, chairperson and chief executive officer of the state-run Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank of the Philippines (AAIIBP), wants to dismantle that misconception. “Faith shaped the principles of Islamic finance, but fairness makes them useful to everyone,” Pangandaman explains to Manila Bulletin. As a former budget chief and central bank assistant governor, Pangandaman brings her macro-level perspective to consumer banking. To her, the appeal of Shari’ah-compliant financing lies in its ethical, transparent, and asset-backed nature, mirroring the modern demand for environmental, social, and governance investing rather than purely religious motivation s. At its core, Islamic finance is treating money not as a commodity that generates interest on its own, but as a medium of exchange tied directly to real economic activity. There are no compounding hidden charges or speculative debt traps, and all transactions are anchored on shared risk and tangible assets. Demystifying financial model To make these concepts practical for the average Filipino, Al-Amanah is stripping away complex Arabic terminology and meeting consumers with simple value propositions. Take home and vehicle loans, for example. Instead of a conventional interest-bearing mortgage, Islamic banking utilizes this concept called Ijarah . In practical terms, Ijarah functions as a lease-to-own arrangement. The bank purchases the asset and leases it to the client for a clear and fixed period, after which ownership transfers smoothly. There are no unpredictable interest rate spikes or hidden penalty fees. For entrepreneurs, conventional banking often poses a barrier due to strict real estate collateral demands. In fact, national data reveal that only about four percent of total bank loans go to micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs). Islamic banking flips this dynamic using models like Murabahah (transparent cost-plus financing) and Musharakah (joint-venture risk sharing). Under Murabahah , if a baker needs new ovens, the bank purchases the equipment and sells it to the business owner at an agreed-upon, upfront profit margin paid over time—allowing the owner to know the exact final cost from day one. Under risk-sharing models like Musharakah , the bank acts more like a partner invested in the growth of the business rather than a lender waiting to seize collateral. “For MSMEs and women entrepreneurs, we replace rigid real estate collateral with Musharakah , Mudarabah , and Murabahah , evaluating businesses on their growth potential rather than existing wealth,” Pangandaman notes. “For equipment and property funding, we offer Ijarah as a clear, lease-to-own alternative without hidden interest charges.” Empowering local, global Filipinos This approach holds immense appeal for two consumer groups: domestic small businesses and overseas Filipino workers (OFWs). Millions of OFWs working in the Middle East and Southeast Asia regularly seek transparent, ethical avenues to buy homes, build local businesses, or invest their savings back in the Philippines. By partnering with agencies like the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA), Al-Amanah is creating digital pathways for overseas workers to access interest-free home financing and ethical savings products without losing money to hidden fee structures. At the same time, domestic business owners, agricultural ventures, and regional cooperatives are discovering that Shari’ah-compliant financing fits their operational reality. Through prospective collaborations with the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) and the Cooperative Development Authority (CDA), working capital and equipment leasing can be extended based on actual cash flow and business viability rather than personal property deeds. Beyond retail consumers, the philosophical overlap between Islamic finance and ESG principles is driving interest from mainstream institutional investors. Concepts like Maslahah (social welfare) and Khalifah (stewardship) directly mandate that capital must avoid harm and contribute positively to society and the environment. “Islamic finance and ESG principles share the same core values: stewardship, social welfare, and avoiding harm,” says Pangandaman. “This makes sustainable financing a natural area for Islamic finance to play a greater role—because the purpose is not simply to finance a project, but to ensure that capital creates a positive and lasting impact on communities and the environment.” Digital growth, regional reach To bring these ethical options to mainstream consumers nationwide, Al-Amanah is pursuing a strategy focused on digital reach and strategic partnerships. While physical expansion continues in places like Tawi-Tawi and Marawi, the bank is prioritizing a robust mobile banking platform. By integrating paperless onboarding using the national PhilSys ID, anyone with a smartphone—whether a farmer in Bukidnon, a shopkeeper in Cebu, or an OFW in Dubai—can open an interest-free savings account or apply for financing. Rather than attempting to compete directly with commercial megabanks, Al-Amanah is collaborating with conventional financial institutions, including its parent entity, the Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP). Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) guidelines now allow commercial banks to establish “Islamic Banking Windows,” opening the door for co-financing large green infrastructure, commercial real estate, and local trade projects through shared-risk frameworks. Furthermore, by tapping into the regional Halal economy across the ASEAN network—a market projected to reach trillions of dollars in the coming years—Al-Amanah aims to serve as a financial bridge connecting Philippine businesses to trade corridors in Malaysia, Indonesia, and beyond. Ultimately, the goal is to offer every Filipino a financial alternative that prioritizes equity, clarity, and genuine economic growth. “At the heart of Islamic finance is the concept of Amanah—a sacred trust,” Pangandaman says. “My goal is to apply macro-level fiscal discipline to personal banking: ensuring that finance builds tangible businesses, creates jobs, and gives every Filipino a stake in national growth without compromising their values.”

2 die after being trapped in Sampaloc house fire. A 78-year-old homeowner and her 48-year-old helper died after being trapped inside a burning house along Don Quijote Street in Sampaloc, Manila, early Saturday morning, August 15. The two were found unconscious and lying on the floor, with police saying they still had pulses when firefighters brought them out. They were rushed to hospitals but were later declared dead. The fire broke out at around 1 a.m. in the two-story house, which relatives said was built in the 1930s, and was declared out at 1:32 a.m. A relative said he was about to use the bathroom when he noticed thick smoke coming from the house. “Akala ko noong una, aircon lang na nagmalfunction at umuusok (At first, I thought it was just the air conditioner malfunctioning and producing smoke),” he said. He immediately brought his family outside before rushing toward the burning house. “Nilabas ko muna yung mag-ina ko, tapos tumakbo ako doon sa kabilang bahay. Pero sobrang kapal na ng usok (I brought my wife and child outside first, then ran to the other house. But the smoke was already very thick),” he said. The family then called firefighters, who reportedly arrived about seven minutes later. By the time responders reached the house, thick smoke had already filled the lower portion of the structure. The doors were also reportedly heavily locked, preventing firefighters from immediately entering through the ground floor. Firefighters instead worked to open a window fitted with metal grills to gain access. After several minutes, they were able to enter and found the two victims unconscious and lying on the floor. Fire responders said the victims still had pulses when they were brought out of the house. They were rushed to hospitals but were later declared dead. The victims reportedly had no visible burns or wounds, raising the possibility that they may have died from smoke inhalation or suffocation. The exact cause of death, however, will have to be determined by the proper authorities. A dog was also found unconscious inside the house. Neighbors desperately tried to revive the animal, with some performing CPR and others attempting mouth-to-mouth resuscitation. It was later brought to a veterinary clinic along Dapitan Street but could no longer be revived. No adjacent structures were reported affected by the fire. Initial information indicated that an electrical problem involving wires may have caused the fire, although authorities have yet to establish the official cause. The incident remains under investigation.

Abra farmer finds decomposing body while gathering mushrooms. TAYUM, Abra — A farmer gathering mushrooms in a forested area of Barangay Bagalay here instead discovered the decomposing body of an unidentified man around noon Wednesday. The farmer immediately reported the grisly discovery to a barangay tanod, who relayed the information to the Tayum Municipal Police Station. Police said their initial assessment indicated that the man may have been dead for three to four days. The unidentified man was estimated to be between 30 and 40 years old, about five feet tall, and was wearing only blue-green shorts when found. Police said no residents in the barangay recognized the victim, raising the possibility that he may have come from another area. There were also no apparent external signs of wounds on the body based on the initial police assessment. The Tayum police are coordinating with other concerned agencies to establish the man’s identity and determine the circumstances surrounding his death. Authorities urged anyone who has a missing family member or may have information that could help identify the deceased to contact the Tayum Municipal Police Station.

Recording Academy holds dialogue with Asian music community over new Grammy category. The Recording Academy has held discussions with members of the Asian music community about the Grammy Awards' new Best Asian Pop Music Performance category, with some artists expressing concerns that the category does not adequately represent their music. In a statement issued Aug. 14, Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. said the organization had spoken with various stakeholders over the past two weeks, including artists and representatives from the K-pop, J-pop, C-pop and Indian music communities. "The Grammy organization exists to serve all music people, and part of that is working to ensure that no voice or community gets overlooked or misunderstood," Mason said. "It’s clear from our numerous conversations with many stakeholders over the past two weeks that, regardless of our intent and desire to be even more inclusive, there are some artists in this space who feel that this category isn’t representing the music they work so hard to create, in the way they wish. As a musician myself, I take that to heart," he added. Mason said the Recording Academy and its board are focused on working with the Asian music community as the organization moves forward. "We are focused on working together to keep pace with that progress and ensure the musicians we intend to honor feel truly seen and heard by our actions," he said. According to Billboard, the discussions involved musicians, labels, managers and representatives from HYBE, the South Korean entertainment company behind K-pop superstars BTS. The Recording Academy is also convening its Board and Awards & Nominations Committee to work with members of the Asian music community and seek their input on the new category. The move comes after BTS announced that the group would not submit entries for this year's Grammy Awards. On July 29, the seven BTS members shared their decision on Instagram Stories. "We have decided not to submit to this year's Grammys. We hope that music can be heard and loved for its own sake, rather than being categorized by region or language. We thank ARMY [fans] and everyone who is always with us," they said. The announcement sparked an online debate, with some fans and music followers supporting BTS' decision while others criticized the group. The Recording Academy announced the Best Asian Pop Music Performance category in June as one of five new categories for the Grammy Awards. According to the academy, the category recognizes "artistic excellence in Asian pop music performances originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets," including K-pop, J-pop and C-pop, with meaningful use of one or more Asian languages. The new category is part of the Recording Academy's effort to recognize music from Asian markets, but the recent discussions suggest that questions remain within the Asian music community about how the category should represent the region's diverse music scene.

Fashion that matters: UNIQLO and its commitment towards improving Filipino lives through Japanese innovation. When two cultures meet, remarkable things happen. A harmonious blend of tradition, innovation, and purpose blooms into a celebration of everything shared between them. It is this very fusion that filled the UNIQLO Manila Global Flagship Store last July 29, in Glorietta 5, Makati City, in celebration of the 70th Anniversary of Philippines and Japan bilateral relations. Lotus flowers in rice terraces. Cranes hovering over coconut trees, and a koi that rides the waves of Siargao. These are the monuments unveiled at "Celebrating Our Friendship: Japanese Innovation for Everyday Filipino Life." Reimagining the country's landscapes with prominent Japanese symbols, amplifying the values shared by the two countries. Created in collaboration with Salcedo Auctions from sustainable components, each installation pays homage to one of the country's three island groups: the Luzon piece pairs the Banaue Rice Terraces with the lotus, a symbol of purity, renewal, and harmony between people and land; the Visayas display sets coconut trees beside a crane, the Japanese symbol of longevity and grace; and the Mindanao installation centers on Siargao's waves, where a koi, Japan's symbol of perseverance, captures resilience. Together, they honor a friendship of 70 years and a brand that has grown with Filipinos for 14 years. Fueling education with LifeWear The celebration goes beyond the store. Through "Supporting Brighter Futures Through Education," a year-long program with ABS-CBN Foundation, HOPE Foundation, and SM Foundation, UNIQLO is supporting 15 schools across the Philippines as it moves toward its 15th anniversary in 2027. The initiative goes beyond infrastructure, covering educational programs, LifeWear donations for students and teachers, volunteer engagement, and community partnerships, with proceeds from selected AIRism products going toward the cause. "Education is a shared responsibility, and meaningful progress is achieved when government, communities, and responsible private sector partners work together," said Department of Education Secretary Sonny Angara. As the brand continues to expand, it ensures that its commitment to social responsibilities grows alongside it. “Success is not measured only by the number of stores we open or the number of customers we serve. It is also measured by the positive differences we make in the communities that have welcomed us for the past fourteen years,” said Geraldine Sia, UNIQLO Philippines Chief Operating Officer. Education is just one thread. Through sustainability, disaster support, and community partnerships, UNIQLO continues to contribute to Philippine society beyond business, creating a brighter future for the next generation. Threads of Filipino craftsmanship The spirit of the milestone lives in stitches. The Re.UNIQLO Special Artisan Patches, created with art director Wilson Limon, bring together three artisan communities, each with its own embroidery language. Itneg weavers from Abra stitched motifs inspired by nature, along with geometric patterns, animals, or human figures - each pattern carrying personal or communal stories. Panay Bukidnon artisans from Iloilo contributed Panubok embroidery rooted in nature, oral traditions, and ancestral beliefs. T'boli weavers from Lake Sebu drew their motifs from mountains, wildlife, and dream imagery that reflect daily life and spiritual traditions. Made with traditional techniques and Re.UNIQLO fabric scraps, each patch gives new life to LifeWear through sustainable practice. Every patch purchased, at PHP 300 each from July 29 onwards, supports the School of Living Traditions. All proceeds from the sale of the patches will be donated back to the community, focused on preserving traditional crafts and livelihoods. This is with the guidance of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts and with UNIQLO’s partnership with the ABS-CBN Foundation. Japanese innovation for Filipino life At the heart of it all is LifeWear, UNIQLO's philosophy of simple, high-quality clothing designed to improve everyday life. Designed for the country's humid climate, Japanese innovation runs through every fiber: AIRism's ultrafine polyester delivers sweat absorption, quick drying, and a smooth, cool-to-the-touch feel with enhanced stretch; UV Protection blocks up to 90 percent of harmful UV rays with Toray's NANODESIGN technology while offering water repellency and durability for tropical weather. DRY-EX uses ergonomic mesh ventilation that enhances airflow, and Miracle Air reimagines business wear with a lightweight, 2-way stretch fabric that delivers the refined look of premium wool without sacrificing comfort. HEATTECH, on the other hand, uses micron-sized fibers that capture the energy of water molecules emitted from the body and convert it into warmth, ideal for cooler climates or overseas travel. "We believe clothing can improve everyday life, but our role extends further than apparel," said Osamu Ikezoe, UNIQLO Philippines Chief Operating Officer, “Through education, environmental initiatives, disaster response, and community partnerships, we hope to create lasting social value and contribute to a brighter future for the next generation of Filipinos.” adding that the brand sees its 15th anniversary as the beginning of a new chapter of growing together with the country. Stitching cultures, building futures Since opening its first store at SM Mall of Asia in 2012, UNIQLO has grown into a network of 81 stores nationwide, carrying functionality, comfort, and timeless style to communities across Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. Through education, craftsmanship, sustainability, and clothing that works for Filipinos, UNIQLO has evolved from a brand into a partner. As it approaches its 15th year, its promise remains unchanged: to do more than dress a nation, but to become part of its better future. Visit the UNIQLO Flagship Store to experience the celebration firsthand, from the monuments and artisan patches to exclusive offerings and the latest LifeWear innovations. For more information, visit www.uniqlo.com/ph/en/ and follow @uniqlo on Facebook and @uniqlophofficial on Instagram and TikTok.

Muntinlupa police serve arrest warrants vs 2 men for illegal drugs, acts of lasciviousness. Venus Williams falls again at Cincinnati Open, singles skid hits 13. MASON, Ohio (AP) — Venus Williams' losing streak in singles play has reached 13 matches. The seven-time major champion was defeated, 6-2, 6-2, by Emiliana Arango on Friday, Aug. 14, in the first round of the Cincinnati Open. The 46-year-old Williams received a wild-card entry to the WTA 1000 event. She has not won a singles match since July 2025. Arango, a 25-year-old qualifier from Colombia ranked 95th, needed 1 hour, 5 minutes to defeat Williams on the grandstand court at Lindner Tennis Center. Williams had her serve broken in the first game of the match and faced an uphill battle the rest of the way. Arango was 4 of 5 on converting break points and won 71% of her first-serve points. Williams was unable to convert on her lone break opportunity and was only 41% on first-serve points. “That kind of eased my nerves a little bit of having maybe a little bit of breathing room. And then I think I just did a good job of staying on it, trying to make her play as much as possible,” Arango said about getting ahead early. Arango will face No. 7 seed and defending Cincinnati champion Iga Swiatek in the second round. Williams' last singles victory came last year in Washington, when she defeated Peyton Stearns. “I think that at all times I was really controlling the point, but unfortunately didn’t finish it the way I wanted to,” said Williams, who is making her 11th appearance in the tournament. “The encouraging part is that I’m controlling the shots, but I have to just get a little more consistent on that last part.” Williams will remain in Cincinnati to play doubles with her sister, Serena, after they received a wild-card entry. They last played doubles together at the 2022 U.S. Open. The Williams sisters were slated to play doubles at Wimbledon before an injury to Serena. They will play Marta Kostyuk and Peyton Stearns in the first round. The doubles portion of the tournament starts Sunday. “I’m excited and hope that we can both go into it fresh, on our toes and ready. I’ll be preparing for that,” Venus Williams said. Venus is also slated to play mixed doubles at the U.S. Open later this month with Alexander Bublik.

Garnett’s No. 21 set for Timberwolves retirement in February. MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — The Minnesota Timberwolves will retire Hall of Fame forward Kevin Garnett's No. 21 jersey after their game against the Boston Celtics this season. The team announced Friday, Aug. 14, that the ceremony will take place following the Feb. 28 game at Target Center against the Celtics, who retired Garnett's jersey in 2022. Garnett will become just the second player in the 37-year history of the franchise to have his number retired, following the late Malik Sealy, a close friend and teammate of Garnett's who died in a car crash in 2000. Garnett had a falling out with former Timberwolves owner Glen Taylor, but the club under new ownership made amends and hired him last year as a team ambassador. He made his first appearance at Target Center in April during the Minnesota's final game of the 2025-26 regular season. Garnett won the NBA MVP award for the 2003-04 season while leading the Timberwolves to the Western Conference finals. After playing the first 12 years of his career for Minnesota, he was traded to the Celtics in 2007 and won an NBA title with them in his first year. He returned to Minnesota in 2015 and played his last of 21 seasons in the league there. Garnett is the all-time Timberwolves leader in numerous statistical categories, including points, rebounds, blocks, assists and steals.

Puerto Rican boxer Prichard Colón dies 11 years after ring tragedy. The boxing world was in mourning Friday, Aug. 14, following the death of Puerto Rican fighter Prichard Colón at the age of 33, 11 years after he sustained brain damage in the only defeat of his professional career. Colón’s death was confirmed in statements by the World Boxing Council and the World Boxing Organization late Thursday. In October 2015, Colón suffered a brain bleed in a light-middleweight fight against Terrel Williams in the Washington, D.C., suburb of Fairfax, Virginia. Colón underwent surgery to relieve pressure on his brain and the WBC said he sustained “irreversible neurological damage” because of what the governing body described as “severe, illegal blows to the back of the head.” He never fought again and was later pictured in a wheelchair. The WBC named him an honorary world champion. “The ‘Champion of the Heart’ became a global symbol of resilience, faith, and dignity,” said the WBC, which added that the incident involving Colón inspired the governing body to reinforce its safety regulations and implement stricter medical protocols. The WBC praised his family for its support in “one of the most moving and outstandingly brave battles for life the world has ever witnessed.” The WBO described Colón as “a warrior until the very end” and said his “courage, strength and fighting spirit transcended the ring.” “His greatest fight became a testament to resilience and the unwavering love of his family,” the WBO added. Before the fight against Williams, Colón collected 16 straight wins, including 13 knockouts. He lost by disqualification against Williams because his cornermen removed his gloves after the 10th round, believing the contest to be over.

P-Beauty: The fourth force in Asian beauty. Recently, I saw local beauty brands like Ever Bilena, Issy, Vice, and Sunnies Face make the headlines, basically covering what’s happening in the Philippines’ cosmetics industry and featuring the ones building it. I’ve since seen more international press start to put P-beauty in the same sentence as K-beauty and J-beauty, and I wanted to explore this further. So I asked Dr. Christine Hall, a UK-based aesthetics doctor known for tracking Korean and Asian beauty science, what she saw from the outside looking in. I first met Dr. Christine through a friend at a coffee shop in BGC in July. She was just as she is on social media: deeply knowledgeable and culturally grounded without ever feeling intimidating. She was kind enough to accommodate my questions. The rise of P-Beauty I asked Dr. Christine where she thought Philippine beauty fit in the broader Asian beauty landscape. “I genuinely believe P-Beauty is the fourth force in Asian beauty,” she told me. When we say Asian beauty, K-beauty, J-beauty, and C-beauty are usually the first ones that come to mind. Each of them has its own distinct identities, ranging from Korean innovations to Japanese rituals and China’s power in scale. “The Philippines has something equally distinctive to contribute, and I think we’re only beginning to see the scale of it.” She pointed out that the Philippines’ tropical climate creates genuinely different skincare needs than the colder markets that shaped K-beauty and J-beauty. Citing heat, humidity, sun exposure, and sweat, these “make P-Beauty much more than just a variation of K-Beauty,” she said. “It can be a response to a different environment, a different culture and a different understanding of beauty. P-Beauty doesn’t need to sit underneath another country’s beauty category. It can stand proudly in its own right.” Don’t copy Korea With K-Pop culture deeply integrated in our society, I thought it would be natural to consult her expertise on best practices that the Philippines can take from how K-beauty went global. “I don’t think the lesson for the Philippines is to copy Korea. Quite the opposite,” she remarked. K-beauty’s rise came from a philosophy around skin health, constant innovation, sharp branding, and an entertainment export machine most countries simply don’t have. But the Philippines, she expressed, already has its own unique proposition. Particularly, “an incredibly engaged domestic audience, a huge and passionate Filipino diaspora, a powerful creator culture, and an enormous amount of pride in Filipino identity.” Social media, she explained, has bridged a gap that a generation ago would have been nearly impossible to close. “The opportunity is to build on what is already uniquely Filipino, not to recreate K-Beauty.” P-Beauty’s relevance to the world “The world is getting warmer, and more consumers are looking for products that perform in heat, humidity, and strong sun,” she replied in response to my query on how P-Beauty can resonate beyond the Philippines. “Lightweight skincare, high-performing sunscreens, sweat-resistant makeup, and formulas designed to feel comfortable in tropical climates aren’t niche requirements anymore. They’re becoming increasingly relevant globally.” She pointed to color and skin tone as well. She called out the morena movement specifically as having “enormous international potential,” and described Filipino makeup’s saturated, confident color palette as “incredibly refreshing” in a region she felt had sometimes leaned toward muted, soft aesthetics. “I don’t just think P-Beauty could resonate internationally. It will.” Filipinos are one of the greatest global communities "Warmth and community are commercial strengths," Dr. Christine said, referring to the edge she thought Filipino brands specifically had. These “create something brands spend enormous amounts of money trying to manufacture,” which she declared was “genuine trust.” She talked about the diaspora as one of the world’s great global communities, and about how a product can build loyalty at home, travel through that diaspora, and resonate with consumers who have no Filipino connection at all, “simply because the product is genuinely good.” Moreover, with P-beauty, affordability and desirability can coexist. “Inclusive shades, accessible prices, and products that genuinely perform aren’t compromises. They can be the reason people want the brand.” P-beauty’s diversity If K-beauty gave the world “glass skin” as shorthand, for Dr. Christine, P-beauty doesn’t need its equivalent of that. “I don’t think P-beauty needs to find its own equivalent of glass skin,” she affirmed that “inclusivity, adaptability, confidence and resourcefulness” are areas that P-beauty can be better known for. “It doesn’t have to mean one particular skin tone, one particular aesthetic, or one particular type of beauty. P-beauty could be about celebrating the incredible diversity of beauty rather than defining what it is supposed to look like.” Beauty flowing back out P-beauty has been around for years, but it took time for Filipinos to shift from an “imported is better” mindset to “proudly local.” I asked if she felt Filipinos needed validation from abroad first before they truly embraced their own brands. She strongly disagreed. “I’d actually gently challenge the premise. I don’t think Filipinos were ever lacking appreciation for their own beauty or creativity,” she said. “What’s changed is visibility.” Ingredients like pili, papaya, and moringa have deep local histories, but what’s new is the platform. She’s seen it in her own audience. Followers with no connection to the Philippines asking her where to buy products she’s featured, simply because the products stand on their own. “For a long time, beauty trends largely flowed into the Philippines. I think we’re starting to see something different now,” Dr. Chrsitne mused. “Beauty is beginning to flow back out. And that’s when you know a beauty movement is becoming genuinely global.”

‘A Very Laufey Day’ returns for fourth year with events in 75 cities. NEW YORK (AP) — It was 2023 when Icelandic singer-songwriter Laufey, known for her neoclassical jazz-pop, decided to create a global fan event. Her second album, “Bewitched,” was about to be released, and she wanted to do something special to celebrate it. More than that, she wanted to encourage her fans to step outside their homes and experience a day inspired by her favorite places and the music from the album. And thus, “A Very Laufey Day” was born. Each year, the Grammy-winning singer curates itineraries for different locations around the world for her listeners to follow. The event allows fans to experience what she describes as “a perfect day” while also connecting with other members of her community offline and in person. Now approaching its fourth edition, the celebration has grown significantly. “It became much bigger than I anticipated, really,” she says. Laufey originally hoped to encourage her audience to discover “third spaces” and explore places she loves, including museums, bookstores, cafes and concert venues. The event has also become an opportunity for fans to build a sense of community, with some dressing in vintage outfits inspired by Laufey’s style. Aug. 23 will mark the fourth annual “A Very Laufey Day.” “It is a fun puzzle every year,” she says. ‘A Very Laufey Day’ 2026 This year’s “A Very Laufey Day” will feature experiences in 75 cities across 25 countries, with the theme “A Celebration of the Arts.” The lineup includes performances involving symphony orchestras, ballet, jazz, opera and theater, along with events at libraries, bookstores, coffee shops, yogurt and ice cream shops, among other venues. Laufey’s concert film, “A Night at the Symphony: Hollywood Bowl,” will also be screened at select theaters. She has partnered with museums around the world, including New York City’s Guggenheim, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago, London’s Tate Modern and National Gallery, Chile’s Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes, Seoul’s Daelim Museum and others. At participating businesses, fans will also have the chance to purchase limited-edition merchandise and Laufey-themed specialty drinks. “This year it was really about focusing on the arts and culture and finding ways to bring this barrier of entry down between my audience — which is mostly Gen Z and Gen A — and these kind of so-called high cultural experiences,” she says. Laufey said the goal is to help her young audience feel more comfortable exploring institutions such as orchestras, museums and galleries. “Whether it’s going to see an orchestra show … museums or galleries, we really want to find ways to connect with those institutions,” she says. For younger fans, some of these cultural spaces can feel intimidating. Laufey said this year’s event was designed to make them feel more welcoming. “It doesn’t have to be this scary thing. And so, I’ve kind of made it my life’s mission to make spaces like that fun and accessible,” she says.

Gilas to field an all-PBA team for Asiad. The coaching staff of Gilas Pilipinas will be juggling their time to train two different compositions of the national team for the upcoming tournaments in the August window of the FIBA World Cup Asian qualifiers and for the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. Gilas head coach Tim Cone has no other choice but to tap PBA players to fill in the missing roles in the team after most members of the original Gilas crew, particularly the overseas players, are not available for the Asiad. “We’re gonna have pretty much two separate teams, one for the window and one for the Asian games. I guess we’ll release that at some point but that’s pretty much the plan,” said Cone. “None of the Japan and Korean players can play in the Asian Games so we just decided that we will field an all-PBA contingent for the Asian Games along with Justin (Brownlee),” he added. Cone, however, intends to focus first on the preparation of Gilas as they begin training for the games against Jordan and Iran on Monday, Aug. 17. The Asiad team will also start its practice at some point with Cone assigning some of his deputies to facilitate the training while Cone is with the Gilas team that will play in the FIBA World Cup Asian qualifiers window. “We’re gonna practice separately at this point,” said Cone. “We have plans for me to handle the window until we get it done and then transfer to the Asiad team. In the meantime, Richard (del Rosario), Josh (Reyes) and Jong (Uichico) will handle the Asian Games,” he added. Cone said some of the PBA stars that will see action in the FIBA window can still be called up for the Asiad team. Some of the league's biggest stars have already been named to the pool like Robert Bolick of NLEX, Sedrick Barefield of Blackwater, Zav Lucero of Magnolia, Adrian Nocum and Caelan Tiongson of Rain or Shine and Jason Perkins of Phoenix. Also part of the 30 names the Samahang Basketbol ng Pilipinas submitted are San Miguel’s Jerrick Ahanmisi and Don Trollano, Converge’s Justin Arana, Meralco’s Brandon Bates and TNT’s Jordan Heading and Brandon Ganuelas-Rosser. PBA players originally part of Gilas are June Mar Fajardo, Scottie Thompson, CJ Perez, RJ Abarrientos, Troy Rosario, Juan Gomez de Liaño, Justine Baltazar and Chris Newsome.

Local lore hunting in El Nido. Apart from exploring places and experiencing different cultures, it is inevitable to meet people when traveling. For some, being in a crowd is part of the fun. But for others, it can be overwhelming, making the off-season more appealing. In the Philippines, when the summer season has its final chapter in late May, many destinations enter their off-season. One such place is the municipality of El Nido in Palawan. Some of its streets, once so crowded during peak season that cars were unable to pass through, become noticeably more relaxed, offering visitors a different side of the popular island destination. While the tropical town’s tourist spots are open for adventure, its less busy period can make local lore hunting a more intimate experience, not just with places and people, but with nature as well. That’s what Bearcat Travel and Yacht Charters aims to introduce when the quieter months hit El Nido: a responsible take on tourism, a people- and place-first approach to travel, and meaningful partnerships with local communities. Co-founded by Windi Tapawan and her husband, Lonely Planet Philippines lead author Greg Bloom, the boutique travel company has been creating immersive experiences that go beyond the usual tourist trail since 2016. During a trip led last June, Manila Bulletin Lifestyle experienced a unique local lore hunt through the itinerary and activities curated by Bearcat Travel and Yacht Charters. A quiet retreat El Nido is dotted with a variety of hotels and accommodations to choose from. Some are located in more commercial areas, while others are tucked away in quieter corners of the municipality. We stayed at the latter, which offered a more private, residential-style alternative to conventional hotels. Lugadia Villas, our home for the duration of the trip, is a destination in its own right. It is close enough to restaurants, markets, and other activities, and is positioned just a short walk from Corong Beach. Unlike conventional hotels, its private spaces, generous interiors, and villa-style amenities make it easy to settle into a slower rhythm. Into the mangroves Local lore hunting is all about exploring the everyday, authentic side of a destination, and our first stop features just that: the rarely seen beauty of El Nido and the people who bring its communities to life. Located in Brgy. New Ibajay, the Dewil Eco-Mangrove Association is a community-led conservation and livelihood project highlighting the area’s 412-hectare mangrove forest. There are a lot of things to do there, from kayaking to bird-watching. But the best way to experience the area is by taking a mangrove tour along the Dewil River. Local guides lead the tour as they explain the different mangrove species and how the ecosystem supports local livelihoods. The tour ends at a boardwalk, built by the community with the help of private companies, providing a closer look at the river’s ecosystem and wildlife. A slower escape An El Nido trip is not complete without a day at the beach. But if you are seeking a more secluded area, heading north of the municipality is the way to go. Located in Brgy. Bucana, Duli Beach has everything you want in a beach escape: serene blue water, golden sand, lush greenery, and a laid-back vibe. We stopped by Taran Beach Club, a new beach, wellness, and stay destination by local travel company Tao Philippines. Apart from the beach and sky, what will lure you in is the site’s architecture. Designed by Filipino designer David Agamos Padadac of Aga Mos, the property combines concrete and bamboo, with sweeping curves inspired by the natural environment. Apart from its wellness spaces for yoga, mobility, stretching, and other body-work sessions, the food, too, is something to experience. What they put on the table highlights its “farm-to-table and sea-to-seat” approach. Make sure to order their smoky, tangy kinilaw, while their Ann’s Ube Jam and Mila’s Peanut Butter Banana shakes are the perfect drinks to have when you just want to soak in the view. Where stories, people, and nature meet Bearcat Travel and Yacht Charters is big on bringing the community together. It hosts a variety of events where locals, tourists, and creatives meet. During that month, it co-presented Fête de la Musique El Nido, turning Lio Beach into a shared stage for musicians and audiences from different backgrounds. The boutique travel company also highlights its environmental commitments through its work with the Centre for Sustainability Philippines and discussions with the Large Marine Vertebrates Research Institute Philippines and the Sulubaai Environmental Foundation. One of the activities that spotlights its efforts was its “Stories from Land, Sea, and Forest” at its newly opened Bearcat Travel Lounge inside the Lio Tourism Estate. It featured Filipino films “Busong,” “Iyo Ang Dagat” (The Sea is Yours), and “The Foresters,” with talkback sessions, allowing viewers to get a deep dive into cultural heritage and a unique perspective on our connection to nature, identity, and home. Brunch on the waters One of the highlights of our trip with Bearcat Travel and Yacht Charters was its Mimosa Brunch Cruise, one of several experiences aboard its flagship vessel, M/Y Isla. The yacht’s other offerings include the Sundowner Cruise, Bacuit Bay Day Cruise, Sunset Splash, and Ultimate Date Night for couples. Priced at P3,650 per person, the Mimosa Brunch Cruise is designed for couples and small groups and is also available for last-minute bookings. From 10:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., guests can enjoy hors d’oeuvres and free-flowing mimosas while sailing through the waters of Bacuit Bay. Those looking to explore beneath the surface can also snorkel, paddle, and float in the bay, making for a leisurely morning that can easily stretch into an afternoon of simply enjoying the sea. To discover more of Bearcat Travel and Yacht Charters’ low-impact inland tours, multi-day expeditions, and bespoke itineraries, visit bearcattravel.com or @bearcattravel on Instagram.

MocaMoca surpasses 20 million active users, expanding access to formal credit in the Philippines. MocaMoca, a digital lending platform operated by SEC-registered Copperstone Lending Inc., has surpassed 20 million active users in the Philippines, marking a milestone in its more than five years of providing secure and transparent digital lending solutions to Filipino borrowers. This comes as more Filipinos turn to regulated digital lenders over informal credit sources. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas' 2025 Consumer Finance and Inclusion Survey found that 16% of adult borrowers now choose formal financial institutions, yet the World Bank's 2025 Global Findex Report shows only about half of Filipino adults hold a formal financial account, below the East Asia and Pacific regional average. TransUnion's Q2 2026 Consumer Pulse Study found that while nearly half of Filipinos intend to apply for credit, 60% abandon the process due to cost, eligibility requirements, or other barriers, highlighting the continued need for accessible and trusted digital lending solutions. MocaMoca is also among the top 10 most-downloaded digital lending apps on Google Play in the Philippines, reflecting sustained demand for the platform. Women account for more than 60% of MocaMoca's borrower base, underscoring the platform’s impact among those managing household and micro-enterprise finances and who have traditionally had limited access to formal credit. "Many Filipinos still face barriers when accessing formal credit. Our goal is to remove those barriers through a lending experience that is simple, transparent, and built around the needs of borrowers, while maintaining the highest standards of responsibility and consumer protection," said David Balamon, Chief Executive Officer of Copperstone Lending Inc. To help address barriers to formal credit, MocaMoca provides collateral-free loans of up to ₱50,000 through a streamlined digital application process requiring only one valid government ID. The platform features 24/7 automated approvals that enable secure fund disbursements in as fast as five minutes. To support long-term financial habits, MocaMoca incorporates a structured credit growth path with scalable limits, transparent terms, and payday-aligned repayment cycles, while direct integrations with GCash, Maya, Coins.ph, and GrabPay ensure disbursements and repayments are convenient and accessible nationwide. “As digital finance continues to evolve, our focus remains on helping more Filipinos access formal credit responsibly. We'll continue investing in responsible innovation that makes borrowing more accessible, transparent, and secure, while supporting the country's broader financial inclusion goals," Balamon added.

'Ganito, Ganyan, Ganoon': A Filipino family drama that refuses to feel familiar. By Margaret Tipton Siytangco The first thing that struck me about "Ganito, Ganyan, Ganoon" was how unlike a typical Filipino family drama it felt. I don’t mean that as a criticism. If anything, I think director Cholo Laurel deliberately wanted us to feel a little unsettled. Paz (Agot Isidro) returns to the Philippines after spending more than two decades in the United States, where she left behind her daughter, Joanne (Jodi Sta. Maria). That reunion is the backbone of the story, but the film refuses to take the familiar route. Usually, when a Filipino mother leaves her family, it’s because she needs to work abroad and support them. Paz didn’t leave out of necessity. She left to chase a dream. That one decision immediately changes how we see her. Then the movie keeps adding little things that make everything feel just a bit different. Paz and her son Matti speak with American accents and mannerisms that make them feel like strangers in their own country. Paz insists on calling her daughter “Joanne” instead of the “Jo” everyone else uses. Joanne seeks help from a psychiatrist, something we still rarely see in Filipino films. Even the casual use of marijuana is presented without fanfare, simply as part of these characters’ lives. None of these choices feels random. Together, they create a family that doesn’t quite fit the image we’re used to seeing in local cinema. I don’t know if making the audience uncomfortable was Laurel’s intention, but it was certainly my experience. The movie kept nudging me out of my comfort zone, not with shocking twists, but with characters and situations that refused to behave the way I expected. That also extends to the characters themselves. Paz is difficult to like, but she’s never reduced to a one-note villain. Joanne has every reason to be angry, but the film doesn’t allow her to become simply “the wronged daughter” either. Both women are given enough layers that you understand where they’re coming from, even if you don’t always agree with them. The one character I wanted more from was Joanne’s father, played by Gardo Versoza. Gardo is effortlessly likable, and it’s easy to see why the film uses him for many of its lighter moments. But I kept waiting for another side of him. Here’s a man whose wife walked away more than twenty years ago, built another life overseas, and then suddenly came back. Yet he accepts almost everything with surprising ease. I wasn’t looking for a shouting match. I just wanted one honest moment where we could see the hurt behind the jokes. That would have made his character even stronger. Then there’s the title. Ganito. Ganyan. Ganoon. The more I rolled those words around in my head, the more they seemed to describe the film itself. People aren’t just one thing. They don’t fit neatly into “good” or “bad.” Families don’t always look the way we think they should. Everyone carries their own version of the truth, and sometimes those truths don’t line up. That’s what stayed with me. Whether you agree with the characters or not, "Ganito, Ganyan, Ganoon" refuses to make life simple. It’s messy, uncomfortable, occasionally frustrating, and very human. In the end, I found myself thinking less about who was right or wrong and more about how complicated families really are.

SHINee’s Key, Onew questioned in ‘Injection Aunt’ investigation. SHINee members Key and Onew have been questioned by South Korean authorities as part of a widening investigation into an alleged unlicensed medical practitioner known as the “Injection Aunt.” The probe has drawn attention in South Korea after several celebrities were linked to the woman, identified by her surname, Lee. Authorities are investigating whether she provided medical services without the required license and whether the people who sought her services knew she was not legally authorized to practice medicine. Key and Onew were among the public figures questioned as police worked to establish how they came into contact with Lee and what they understood about her professional credentials. The controversy first gained major attention after comedian Park Na-rae was called in for questioning in May over allegations involving medication she allegedly received from Lee. The investigation has since expanded to other personalities who may have received treatment or medication from the woman. Griffin Entertainment, Onew's agency, said the SHINee singer had been referred to a clinic where he believed Lee was a doctor or a medical professional affiliated with the facility. According to the agency, Onew sought skin care treatment and had no reason to suspect that Lee lacked a valid medical license. Griffin also said Onew had already cooperated with investigators and provided an account of his interactions with Lee. The agency appealed for restraint while authorities continue their investigation, warning against speculation or claims that do not match the facts established by investigators. SM Entertainment had previously commented on Key's involvement in the controversy. The agency said Key only discovered that Lee was allegedly not a doctor after the issue surrounding her medical license became public. It added that the SHINee member was “very confused and deeply regrets his lack of awareness.” Key had taken a break from entertainment activities beginning in December 2025 and returned to the spotlight in May with SHINee's sixth EP, “Atmos.” South Korean authorities are examining whether Lee treated people in locations including officetels and vehicles and allegedly provided prescription medication without the proper authority. Practicing medicine without a license can carry criminal penalties in South Korea. Investigators are also looking into whether individuals who received services from Lee were aware of her alleged lack of credentials. The probe remains ongoing, and no final determination has been made regarding the celebrities' involvement or what they knew about Lee's professional status.

DBP to push for deposit expansion. State-owned Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP) is undertaking an aggressive deposit generation campaign to widen its funding base to support its various lending activities, a top official said. DBP President and Chief Executive Officer Michael O. de Jesus said the Bank has launched a “Save 2 Win” promotion to generate fresh deposits from both individual and institutional depositors to expand in financing activities geared towards high-impact developmental projects. “We believe every deposit entrusted to DBP will help strengthen its capacity to finance transformative projects that will support economic growth, create jobs, and improve the lives of communities across the country,” de Jesus said. DBP is the tenth largest bank in the country with total assets of P1.036 trillion and provides credit support to four priority sectors of the economy – infrastructure and logistics; micro, small and medium enterprises; the environment; and social services and community development. De Jesus said the campaign is expected to widen DBP’s deposit base, which grew by 15.51% to P413.41 billion in the second quarter of the year from P357.91 billion for the same period last year. He said that the campaign offers cash prizes of up to P250,000 to winning individual depositors and gift certificates to winning institutional depositors, which also aims to promote greater financial inclusion, especially among underbanked and unbanked segments of the population. “We hope to inspire more Filipinos to save not only for achieving their personal financial goals but also for contributing to nation-building and achieving sustainable progress,” he added. The “Save 2 Win” promo is open to eligible depositors in all DBP branches nationwide and will run until December 31, 2026. Mechanics of the promotion can be accessed through the DBP website (www.dbp.ph).

PhilHealth rises together with global and strategic partners for the coordinated success of universal health care under the RISE30 mission. The Department of Health (DOH), and the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) presented a 16-month runway of shared reforms aimed at advancing not only PhilHealth's RISE30 Mission, but also improving access, equity, and efficiency in Universal Health Care (UHC) delivery across the Philippines. More than 100 participants, including global development partners, financial institutions, academe, foundations, civil society organizations, other government oversight agencies, and stakeholders, as well as PhilHealth officers and technical staff, convened today at the Asian Development Bank (ADB) Headquarters to align resources and technical expertise behind UHC reforms. Co-sponsored by the ADB through its Build Universal Health Coverage (BUHC) Project, the 2026 PhilHealth Partners' Forum was led by DOH Acting Secretary, Dr. Edwin M. Mercado, Acting PhilHealth President and CEO, Dr. Beverly Lorraine C. Ho, and ADB Country Director Andrew Jeffries. The forum facilitated direct alignment of partner resources and expertise with the sector's Shared Agenda and PhilHealth's multi-year Technical Assistance (TA) Agenda. The program also featured a tribute honoring the coordinated success of PhilHealth and its partners over the past 18 months, recognizing the collective effort behind the gains made in advancing UHC reforms. Primary Care Champion and Department of Finance Secretary, Frederick D. Go, expressed his support for, and confidence in the agencies' shared agenda. ADB Director of the Human and Social Development Sector Office, and former PhilHealth President and CEO, Dr. Eduardo Banzon, commended the progress PhilHealth has made over the past year. PhilHealth recognizes both leaders as pillars of support of the Build UHC Program, whose continued partnership has been instrumental in driving the impact and reach of PhilHealth's programs nationwide. Looking ahead, PhilHealth remains fully committed to building this ecosystem of support alongside the Department of Health. With primary care as the backbone of UHC, the TA Agenda continues to build on the strong collaboration in long-term planning and further expands the partner network in support of ongoing UHC reforms. To ensure the success of these outcomes, PhilHealth laid down the pathway for stakeholders to provide their continued support and active engagement toward this shared, coordinated success.

'The End of Oak Street': A mish-mash of various inspirations with the right amount of heart. Right out of the gate, "The End of Oak Street" presents a bit of a wacko, sci-fi concept, but if you give it a chance, the movie definitely delivers. The movie follows a family in their struggle for survival when their home, and the entirety of the titular Oak Street, suddenly and inexplicably gets transported into the past, when dinosaurs roamed the earth. The parents, Denise and Greg Platt, played by Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor, go from navigating a troubled relationship to fending off feathered reptilian predators, literally overnight. And yes, you read that right, the dinosaurs in "End of Oak Street" are not the kind you would see in any 80’s textbook, even though that’s when the movie initially takes place. While you can still spot a scaled stegosaurus and what was possibly a variant of an ankylosaur, a large number of the dinosaurs are furry and feathery, which brings them closer to today’s more accepted and updated depictions, scientifically speaking. It is a jarring change that lasts for a moment, and just as you might be wondering how dangerous a giant chicken could really be, one of them devours a hapless victim and you get your answer. You know full well going in that there are going to be dinosaurs, but the film very methodically sets up the stakes first before we get a glimpse at them. The Platts, along with their children Audrey and Brian (Maisey Stella and Christian Convery) form the typical American family. But underneath it all the cracks have been forming for some time, with Greg having to take odd jobs to make ends meet and Denise suffering from a feeling of restlessness. The undoubtedly unusual circumstances cause even more strain, and the battle is not only to survive, but to keep going and survive together. Despite the tight 90 minute runtime, the dinosaurs don’t really show up till a good 20 to 30 minutes in. But the time isn’t wasted. Instead they lurk in the periphery of your vision, just a shadow off to the side, or a form that you just missed, building up a suspense that feels doubly intense as the idyllic, sunny suburban vibes contrast sharply with the stark horror of impending doom. Of course the obvious point of comparison here is "Jurassic Park." Those involved knew for sure that their film would be held up side by side with the Spielberg classic, and they weren’t shy about it, even leaning into the comparison by giving little nods to the ‘90s film. Perhaps because it was set in the 80’s when things were clearer and life was simpler, there is also something reminiscent of the "Twilight Zone" about the movie, in how the unknown slowly creeps into the familiar. It’s at the same time eerie and horrifying. Much like the "Twilight Zone," there really is no explanation given as to the cause of the anomaly. There’s a theory, some advanced science thrown around like it was simple algebra, but there was nothing definitive. There was no expert saying this is what happened, no secret device that explained the whole reason for the event, nothing. it was an unexplained blip and the movie is better for it. You don’t spend too much time wondering and worrying about it because, well, your main concern is not becoming dino-dinner. An explanation would have taken the attention away from the core of the story. No, not the dinos, as impressive-looking as they are. But the core of the film is the family dynamic. Hathaway and McGregor both deliver great performances, and compliment each other in their roles, with Mcgregor playing the dad as more positive and eternally optimistic, while Hathaway played her role as more pragmatic and decisive. It is a subtle point but you quickly see who wears the pants in the family as in the film McGregor often has something to hit with while Hathaway ends up with a rifle in her hands, every bit the imposing mother protecting her cubs. All in all the movie is a mish-mash of various inspirations and tropes, but they do mish and mash quite wonderfully. It has great visuals, plenty of suspense and action, and the right amount of heart. And yes, tons of dinosaurs too.

LANDBANK honors outstanding partners, clients at 2026 Gawad TANYAG Awards. LANDBANK honored outstanding clients and institutional partners during its 2026 Gawad TANYAG (Tanging Yaman at Galing) Awards, held on 7 August 2026 as part of the Bank’s 63rd anniversary celebration. The ceremony recognized exemplary farmers and fishers, cooperatives, micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), corporations, countryside financial institutions (CFIs), and microfinance institutions (MFIs) for their contributions to community development and inclusive growth. Finance Secretary and LANDBANK Chair Frederick D. Go underscored the crucial role of the awardees in national development. "Sa loob ng mahigit anim na dekada, kayo ay naging mahalagang katuwang ng LANDBANK sa pagsusulong ng pambansang kaunlaran. Kasama ang ating mga magsasaka at mangingisda, kooperatiba, MSMEs, at mga institusyong pampinansyal, patuloy ninyong pinalalawak ang mga oportunidad na nagbibigay-lakas sa mga komunidad at nag-aambag sa pag-unlad ng ating bansa," he said in a statement. LANDBANK President and CEO Lynette V. Ortiz led the ceremony alongside Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) Secretary Francis N. Tolentino, National Treasurer Sharon P. Almanza, and key development partners. "For decades, LANDBANK has stayed true to its identity as the people’s bank, because people have always been at the heart of everything we do. And so, the true wealth of this institution is not in our balance sheets — it lives in every farmer and fisherfolk, every cooperative, every enterprise, and partner that turns hard work into shared prosperity," LANDBANK President and CEO Ortiz said. In his keynote address, Labor Secretary Tolentino highlighted the broader impact of the awardees' accomplishments on Filipino families and communities. “Ang inyong mga tagumpay ay hindi lamang nasusukat sa paglago ng inyong organisasyon o kabuhayan. Nasusukat din ito sa dami ng oportunidad na inyong nalilikha, sa mga trabahong inyong nasusuportahan, at sa mga pamilyang nagkakaroon ng mas magandang kinabukasan dahil sa inyong mga pagsisikap,” he said. Honoring champions of progress Among the awardees under the Gawad PITAK (Pinakatanging Kooperatiba) category were Nagkakaisang Magsasaka Agricultural Primary Multi-Purpose Cooperative, Caviteño Isabelino Multipurpose Cooperative, Kaagapay Agrarian Reform Cooperative, Barangka Credit Cooperative, and Ating Ani Nueva Ecija Multipurpose Cooperative for excellence in cooperative leadership and community empowerment. The Ulirang Magsasaka and Ulirang Mangingisda awards were conferred on Deodany L. Cara and Teodulo C. Llego, respectively, for their contributions to the agriculture and fisheries sectors. Accepting the award, Cara expressed gratitude for the Bank’s continued support to farmers, emphasizing that agriculture remains a viable path to a brighter future. “Sabi nila walang yumayaman sa pagsasaka. 3 held in separate Parañaque police operations; gun, gambling bets seized. Three persons were arrested in separate police operations in Parañaque City on Friday night, Aug. 14, resulting in the seizure of an unlicensed revolver and cash used as bets in an illegal gambling game. Police identified those arrested as Reggie, 46, of Barangay San Dionisio; Ricky, 50, of Barangay Tambo; and alias Delon, 36, a cook and resident of Bacoor City, Cavite. Ricky and Delon were arrested by personnel of the Tambo Police Substation at around 10:40 p.m. while police were conducting a routine mobile patrol along MIA 3 held in separate Parañaque police operations; gun, gambling bets seized Road. Police said the two were caught playing “cara y cruz,” an illegal coin-tossing gambling game. Officers recovered P970 in various denominations allegedly used as gambling bets, as well as three P1 coins reportedly used as flippers in the game. A .38-caliber revolver loaded with one ammunition was also found in Ricky’s possession. Meanwhile, San Dionisio police officers responded to a report from a concerned citizen about a man allegedly causing a disturbance and carrying a firearm along Baui Street in Tramo Dos. The responding officers arrived at about 11:00 p.m. and found Reggie shouting in public. Police also noticed what appeared to be a firearm bulge at his waistline, leading to his arrest. Ricky and Delon were charged with violating Presidential Decree 1602, or the law against illegal gambling, while Ricky also faces a separate charge under Republic Act 10591, or the Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act. VP Sara’s camp asks court to defer possible arrest warrant, says ‘all options’ open. Vice President Sara Duterte’s legal team has asked a Quezon City court to defer the issuance of an arrest warrant while it considers her motion to quash the three grave threats cases filed against her, saying the court must first resolve the defense’s jurisdictional challenge. Lawyer Paul Lawrence Lim, Duterte’s counsel for the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Grave Threats cases, said deferment of an arrest warrant is among the reliefs sought by the defense in its motion to quash. “The deferment of arrest warrant is one of the things that we asked from the court,” Lim said in a mix of English and Filipino during a virtual press conference on August 14. Lim said the defense’s position is anchored on its argument that the court must first determine whether it has jurisdiction over the cases before proceeding with the criminal proceedings. “And what I can say is that the issuance of a warrant is an exercise of jurisdiction,” he said. The defense has also asked the court to hear oral arguments on the motion to quash, citing the “far-reaching consequences” of the constitutional and legal questions raised by the cases. READ: https://mb.com.ph/2026/08/14/duterte-camp-seeks-oral-arguments-on-motion-to-quash-grave-threats-cases Will Duterte surrender if a warrant is issued? Asked whether Duterte would voluntarily surrender if the court rejects her motion to quash and subsequently issues an arrest warrant, Lim declined to commit on behalf of the Vice President. Lim said the defense has yet to make a final decision on the specific action or remedy it would pursue should the court reject the motion to quash. “We still don’t have a final decision regarding the actual actions and the available remedies that we have,” Lim said. “There are a lot of remedies that are available,” he added, noting that these could include surrendering or questioning the court’s order. “As of now, I cannot say, but all options are being considered,” Lim said. Lim said the legal team has discussed the possible remedies available to Duterte but would determine which one to pursue depending on the court’s action. Defense challenges court jurisdiction Duterte’s motion to quash seeks the dismissal of the criminal cases before arraignment, with the defense arguing that the court “lacks jurisdiction.” The cases stem from Duterte’s remarks during a November 2024 online press conference concerning an alleged assassination plot involving President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez. The defense has argued that the cases raise broader constitutional questions concerning the criminal prosecution of a sitting impeachable official. Lim said the defense’s position is that an “impeachable official may eventually be prosecuted if the official committed a crime, but that such prosecution should take place after the official’s term.” The defense is also seeking oral arguments on the motion to quash, saying the constitutional and jurisdictional questions at issue have potentially far-reaching implications. Lim said the defense wants “oral arguments so both sides can fully present their positions on those questions before the court resolves the motion.” For now, Lim said the legal team is waiting for the court to act on the motion to quash and its request for oral arguments. The defense will then determine its next legal move based on the court’s ruling, including whether the motion to quash is granted or denied and whether an arrest warrant is eventually issued. GMA looks to AI to expand digital experiences for audiences. GMA Network is looking to emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) to expand how it connects with audiences beyond traditional television.
